name: Chemistry
tagline: What everything is made of, and how it changes.

nodes.title: Stuff Around Us
nodes.goal: Notice materials: wood, metal, water, air.
nodes.kid_text: Everything you can touch is made of some kind of stuff called a material. A wooden chair is made of wood, a spoon can be made of metal, and the rain is made of water. Even the air you can't see is real stuff, because you can feel it push when you wave your hand! Look around and name what each thing is made of.

quiz.prompt: What is a spoon made of? 🥄
choices: Metal
Water
Air
quiz.answer: Metal
quiz.say: What is a shiny spoon made of? Is it metal, water, or air?
quiz.explain: Yes! A spoon is made of metal, hard and shiny and cold.

quiz.prompt: Which one is water? 💧 🪵 🔑
quiz.say: Which picture shows water? The drop, the piece of wood, or the key?
quiz.explain: That's right, the little drop is water, wet and runny.

quiz.prompt: Wave your hand. What pushes back? 🖐️
choices: Air
Rock
Wood
quiz.answer: Air
quiz.say: When you wave your hand, something you can't see pushes back. Is it air, rock, or wood?
quiz.explain: Air is real stuff, even though we can't see it!

quiz.prompt: A tree trunk is made of... 🌳
choices: Wood
Metal
Water
quiz.answer: Wood
quiz.say: A big tree trunk. Is it made of wood, metal, or water?
quiz.explain: Trees are made of wood, the same stuff as a wooden chair.

quiz.prompt: What fills a rainy puddle? 🥾
choices: Water
Wood
Metal
quiz.answer: Water
quiz.say: A puddle after the rain. Is it full of water, wood, or metal?
quiz.explain: Puddles are made of water, wet and runny and splashy.

quiz.prompt: Which one is metal? 🍃 💧 🔑
quiz.say: Which picture shows metal? The leaf, the water drop, or the key?
quiz.explain: The key is metal, hard and shiny and cold to touch.

quiz.prompt: What do we breathe in? 👃
choices: Sand
Air
Milk
quiz.answer: Air
quiz.say: When you take a big breath, what goes in your nose? Sand, air, or milk?
quiz.explain: We breathe air! It is real stuff, even though we cannot see it.

nodes.title: Mixing
nodes.goal: See what happens when you mix things.
nodes.kid_text: When you put two things together, sometimes they mix and sometimes they don't. Stir sugar into water and it disappears, but the water tastes sweet, so the sugar is still there hiding! Pour oil into water and it floats on top in yellow blobs instead. Try mixing things and watch which ones join up and which stay apart.

quiz.prompt: Stir sugar into water. What happens? 🥄💧
choices: Disappears
Floats on top
Sinks as lumps
quiz.answer: Disappears
quiz.say: You stir sugar into water. Which happens: it disappears, it floats on top, or it sinks as lumps?
quiz.explain: The sugar disappears into the water, but it's still hiding in there!

quiz.prompt: The water tastes sweet. Sugar still there? 😋
choices: Yes
No
quiz.answer: Yes
quiz.say: After you stir in the sugar, the water tastes sweet. Is the sugar still there? Yes, or no?
quiz.explain: Yes! We can't see it, but we can taste it, so it's still there.

quiz.prompt: Pour oil in water. Oil goes where? 💛💧
choices: Top
Bottom
Middle
quiz.answer: Top
quiz.say: You pour yellow oil into water. Does the oil go to the top, the bottom, or the middle?
quiz.explain: Oil floats up on top in blobs and never mixes in.

quiz.prompt: Stir cocoa powder into milk 🍫🥛
choices: Mixes in
Stays a lump
Floats on top
quiz.answer: Mixes in
quiz.say: You stir chocolate powder into milk. Which happens: it mixes in, it stays a lump, or it floats on top?
quiz.explain: The powder mixes right in and makes the whole drink chocolatey.

quiz.prompt: Sand in water sinks to the... 🏖️💧
choices: Bottom
Top
Middle
quiz.answer: Bottom
quiz.say: You stir sand into a jar of water. Does the sand go to the bottom, the top, or the middle?
quiz.explain: Sand does not mix in. It sinks down and sits at the bottom.

quiz.prompt: Mix red and blue paint. You get... 🎨
choices: Purple
Green
Yellow
quiz.answer: Purple
quiz.say: You mix red paint with blue paint. Do you get purple, green, or yellow?
quiz.explain: Red and blue mix together to make lovely purple paint.

quiz.prompt: Shake oil and water. Stay mixed? 🫙
choices: Yes
No
quiz.answer: No
quiz.say: You shake oil and water together, then wait. Do they stay mixed? Yes, or no?
quiz.explain: No! The oil floats back up into blobs on top every time.

nodes.title: Ice, Water, Steam
nodes.goal: Watch water freeze, melt and boil.
nodes.kid_text: Water can change its shape when it gets hot or cold. In the freezer it turns hard and cold into ice, and when the ice warms up it melts back into runny water. If you heat water very hot on the stove, it bubbles and turns into steam that floats away like a cloud. Cold makes water hard, and heat makes it melt and then boil!

quiz.prompt: Ice in the warm sun becomes... ☀️🧊
choices: Water
Steam
Snow
quiz.answer: Water
quiz.say: You leave an ice cube in the warm sun. Does it turn into water, into steam, or into snow?
quiz.explain: Warm sun melts ice into runny water. It needs to be much hotter to make steam.

quiz.prompt: Where does water turn into ice? 🧊
choices: Freezer
Oven
Sunny window
quiz.answer: Freezer
quiz.say: Where does water get cold and turn hard into ice? In the freezer, in the oven, or on a sunny window?
quiz.explain: The freezer is very cold, and cold makes water turn into hard ice.

quiz.prompt: Very hot bubbling water makes... 🫖
choices: Steam
Ice
Snow
quiz.answer: Steam
quiz.say: When water gets very hot and bubbly on the stove, what floats away? Steam, ice, or snow?
quiz.explain: Hot water boils and turns into steam that floats up like a cloud.

quiz.prompt: A snowman in warm sun will... ⛄☀️
choices: Melt
Freeze
Get bigger
quiz.answer: Melt
quiz.say: A snowman is standing in the warm sun. Will it melt, freeze, or get bigger?
quiz.explain: Warm sun makes snow melt into runny water.

quiz.prompt: Juice left in the freezer gets... 🧃❄️
choices: Hard
Runny
Warm
quiz.answer: Hard
quiz.say: You leave a cup of juice in the freezer all night. Does it get hard, runny, or warm?
quiz.explain: Cold makes drinks freeze hard, just like water turns to ice.

quiz.prompt: Steam is water that is very... 🍲
choices: Very hot
Very cold
Very hard
quiz.answer: Very hot
quiz.say: Steam puffs up from a boiling pot. Is that water very hot, very cold, or very hard?
quiz.explain: Steam comes from very hot water bubbling on the stove.

quiz.prompt: Which one is hard and cold? 🧊 💧 ☁️
quiz.say: Which one is hard and cold? The ice cube, the water drop, or the puff of steam?
quiz.explain: Ice is hard and cold. Water is runny, and steam is a warm cloud.

nodes.title: Solids, Liquids, Gases
nodes.goal: Sort matter by its state and describe each.
nodes.kid_text: Everything is a solid, a liquid, or a gas. A solid like a block keeps its own shape and you can hold it. A liquid like juice is runny and takes the shape of its cup. A gas like air spreads out everywhere and you usually can't see it. Try sorting your toys, your drink, and a balloon's air into the three groups!

quiz.prompt: Juice in a cup is a... 🧃
choices: Solid
Liquid
Gas
quiz.answer: Liquid
quiz.say: Runny juice that takes the shape of its cup. Is it a solid, a liquid, or a gas?
quiz.explain: Juice is a liquid, so it's runny and fits the shape of any cup.

quiz.prompt: What fills a balloon? 🎈
choices: Gas
Liquid
Solid
quiz.answer: Gas
quiz.say: A puffy balloon is filled with air. Is air a gas, a liquid, or a solid?
quiz.explain: Air is a gas, and gases spread out to fill up all the space.

quiz.prompt: A wooden block is a... 🧱
choices: Solid
Liquid
Gas
quiz.answer: Solid
quiz.say: A hard block you can hold in your hand. Is it a solid, a liquid, or a gas?
quiz.explain: A block is a solid, so it keeps its own shape wherever you put it.

quiz.prompt: Which one keeps its own shape? 🪨🥛💨
choices: Rock
Milk
Steam
quiz.answer: Rock
quiz.say: Which one always keeps its own shape? A rock, some milk, or steam?
quiz.explain: A rock is a solid, so it keeps its shape wherever you put it.

quiz.prompt: Steam from a kettle is a... ☕
choices: Solid
Gas
Liquid
quiz.answer: Gas
quiz.say: Steam puffing out of a kettle and spreading around. Is it a solid, a gas, or a liquid?
quiz.explain: Steam is a gas, so it spreads out into all the room.

quiz.prompt: Pour milk in a new cup. Its shape... 🥛
choices: Changes to fit it
Keeps its old shape
Turns hard
quiz.answer: Changes to fit it
quiz.say: You pour milk into a different shaped cup. Which happens: it changes to fit it, it keeps its old shape, or it turns hard?
quiz.explain: Liquids change shape to fit whatever cup they are in.

quiz.prompt: Solid, liquid, gas. How many states? 🔢
quiz.say: Solid, liquid, and gas. How many states of matter is that? 3, 2, or 5?
quiz.explain: There are three: solids, liquids, and gases.

nodes.title: Changing Matter
nodes.goal: Melting, freezing, dissolving and burning.
nodes.kid_text: Stuff can change from one form to another. When ice gets warm it melts into water, and when water gets very cold it freezes back into ice. Stir salt into water and it dissolves, seeming to vanish, but it is still there. When wood burns, it changes into ash and smoke and can never turn back. Watch how heat and mixing make things change!

quiz.prompt: Stir salt into water. It... 🧂💧
choices: Dissolves
Floats
Bounces
quiz.answer: Dissolves
quiz.say: You stir salt into water and it seems to vanish. Which happens: it dissolves, it floats, or it bounces?
quiz.explain: The salt dissolves and hides in the water, but it's still in there.

quiz.prompt: Burning wood turns into... 🔥🪵
choices: Ash
Ice
Juice
quiz.answer: Ash
quiz.say: When wood burns in a fire, what is left behind? Ash, ice, or juice?
quiz.explain: Burning wood leaves grey ash and smoke floating away.

quiz.prompt: Can ash turn back into wood? 🪵
choices: Yes
No
quiz.answer: No
quiz.say: Once wood has burned into ash, can the ash turn back into wood? Yes, or no?
quiz.explain: No, burning is a change that can never go backwards.

quiz.prompt: Ice cream in the hot sun will... 🍦☀️
choices: Melt
Freeze
Get harder
quiz.answer: Melt
quiz.say: You leave ice cream out in the hot sun. Will it melt, freeze, or get harder?
quiz.explain: Heat makes ice cream melt into a drippy puddle.

quiz.prompt: A cup of water left in the ice box all night will… 🌙
choices: Freeze
Boil
Stay runny
quiz.answer: Freeze
quiz.say: You put a cup of water in the ice box overnight. Will it freeze, boil, or stay runny?
quiz.explain: Cold makes water freeze into hard ice.

quiz.prompt: Which change can go backwards? 🔁
choices: Melting
Burning
Toasting bread
quiz.answer: Melting
quiz.say: Which change can go backwards again? Melting, burning, or toasting bread?
quiz.explain: Melted ice can freeze again, but burnt and toasted things never come back.

quiz.prompt: Stir cocoa in warm milk. It... 🍫
choices: Dissolves
Bounces
Floats on top
quiz.answer: Dissolves
quiz.say: You stir cocoa into warm milk and it seems to vanish. Which happens: it dissolves, it bounces, or it floats on top?
quiz.explain: The cocoa dissolves and hides in the milk, but you can still taste it.

nodes.title: Properties of Materials
nodes.goal: Hard, soft, magnetic, see-through: choose the right stuff.
nodes.kid_text: Different materials are good at different jobs. A window is made of glass because you can see through it, and a hammer is made of hard metal so it won't break. A pillow is soft for your head, and a magnet sticks to some metals but not to wood. When you build or fix something, pick the material with the right powers for the job!

quiz.prompt: Which one can you see through? 🏠
choices: Glass
Brick
Wood
quiz.answer: Glass
quiz.say: Windows let you see outside. Are they made of glass, brick, or wood?
quiz.explain: Glass is see-through, so it's perfect for a window.

quiz.prompt: A magnet sticks to... 🧲
choices: Metal
Wood
Cloth
quiz.answer: Metal
quiz.say: A magnet sticks to some things but not others. Does it stick to metal, wood, or cloth?
quiz.explain: Magnets grab onto some metals, but wood and cloth just slip away.

quiz.prompt: Which is soft for your head? 😴
choices: Pillow
Wooden board
Glass plate
quiz.answer: Pillow
quiz.say: Which one is soft and comfy for your head? A pillow, a wooden board, or a glass plate?
quiz.explain: A pillow is soft, so it's the right stuff for resting your head.

quiz.prompt: Best stuff for a raincoat? ☔
choices: Plastic
Paper
Wool
quiz.answer: Plastic
quiz.say: You want a coat that keeps the rain off. Should it be plastic, paper, or wool?
quiz.explain: Plastic keeps water out. Paper would go soggy and tear, and wool soaks the rain right up.

quiz.prompt: A magnet will NOT stick to... 🧲
choices: Plastic
Iron nail
Steel spoon
quiz.answer: Plastic
quiz.say: A magnet will not stick to one of these. Is it the plastic, the iron nail, or the steel spoon?
quiz.explain: Magnets grab iron and steel, but plastic just slides away.

quiz.prompt: Which one is squishy and soft? 🤏
choices: Sponge
Brick
Wooden block
quiz.answer: Sponge
quiz.say: Which one squishes when you press it? A sponge, a brick, or a wooden block?
quiz.explain: A sponge is soft and squishy, but a brick and a block stay hard.

quiz.prompt: Best stuff for a warm hat? 🧢
choices: Wool
Glass
Ice
quiz.answer: Wool
quiz.say: You need a cosy hat for a cold day. Should it be wool, glass, or ice?
quiz.explain: Wool is soft and warm, just right for a hat.

nodes.title: Atoms and Elements
nodes.goal: Everything is built from about a hundred elements.

quiz.prompt: Gold, oxygen, and iron are all examples of chemical elements. What makes something an element?
quiz.answer: A substance made of only one kind of atom, not separable by chemistry
quiz.explain: An element consists of a single type of atom, so ordinary chemical reactions cannot split it into anything simpler. Pure water is a pure substance but not an element.
choices: A substance made of only one kind of atom, not separable by chemistry
Any pure substance, whether it holds one kind of atom or several
Any hard, shiny material that conducts both heat and electricity well
A material holding two or more different substances mixed up together

quiz.prompt: Roughly how many different chemical elements are there that everything in the ordinary world is built from?
quiz.answer: About 100
quiz.explain: The periodic table holds around 100 naturally occurring and stable elements from which all ordinary matter is assembled.
choices: About 100
About 1,000
About 10

quiz.prompt: Water is built from hydrogen and oxygen. Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Table salt is built from sodium and chlorine. Counting each element just once, how many different elements are named here?
quiz.explain: Hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sodium and chlorine make five. Oxygen is named twice, but it is still one element.

quiz.prompt: Imagine cutting a bar of pure iron in half, then cutting one half in half, again and again with a perfect blade. What would the smallest piece that is still iron be?
quiz.answer: One iron atom, the smallest piece still iron
choices: One iron atom, the smallest piece still iron
A speck of iron dust, just big enough to see
Half an iron atom, sliced one more time
There is no smallest piece, because iron goes on forever
quiz.explain: An atom is the smallest piece of an element. Split an iron atom and the bits are protons, neutrons and electrons, which are not iron.

quiz.prompt: Three jars hold copper, sulfur and table salt. Each looks like one pure substance, but only one of them is a compound rather than an element. Which jar, and how could you tell?
quiz.answer: The salt, because it is built from sodium and chlorine chemically joined
choices: The copper, because a metal is really several metals mixed together
The sulfur, because burning it gives off a gas that must have been inside it
The salt, because it dissolves away to nothing in warm water
The salt, because it is built from sodium and chlorine chemically joined
quiz.explain: Table salt is sodium chloride, two elements bonded into one new substance. Dissolving is not the test, and burning sulfur takes its oxygen from the air, not from inside the sulfur.

quiz.prompt: Which list contains nothing but chemical elements?
quiz.answer: Gold, helium and iron
choices: Air, water and fire
Gold, helium and iron
Salt, sugar and chalk
Steel, brass and bronze
quiz.explain: Air is a mixture, water and salt are compounds, and steel and brass are metals blended together. Only gold, helium and iron are single elements.

quiz.prompt: A water molecule holds 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. How many atoms are there in 5 water molecules altogether?
quiz.explain: Each molecule has 3 atoms, and 5 x 3 = 15.

quiz.prompt: A carbon atom has 6 protons. How many electrons does a neutral carbon atom hold?
quiz.explain: A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, so 6.

quiz.prompt: A block of pure copper is heated, hammered flat and then dissolved in acid. What happens to its copper atoms through all of that?
quiz.answer: They stay copper atoms throughout.
choices: They stay copper atoms throughout.
They split when hammered thin.
They turn into a different element when heated strongly.
They break down into simpler atoms once dissolved.
quiz.explain: Chemical and physical treatments rearrange atoms but do not change what element an atom is.

quiz.prompt: Two jars have lost their labels. One holds an element and the other a compound. Which test tells them apart?
quiz.answer: See whether the substance can be broken down chemically into simpler substances.
choices: See whether the substance can be broken down chemically into simpler substances.
See which one dissolves faster in warm water.
See which one is heavier for the same volume.
See which one melts at the lower temperature.
quiz.explain: An element cannot be split into anything simpler by chemical means; a compound can be broken into its elements.

nodes.title: Molecules and Compounds
nodes.goal: How atoms join into molecules.

quiz.prompt: A water molecule is written H2O. What does this tell you about how it is built?
quiz.answer: Two hydrogen atoms are joined to one oxygen atom
quiz.explain: The formula H2O means each molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms bonded to 1 oxygen atom.
choices: One hydrogen atom is joined to two oxygen atoms
Two hydrogen atoms are joined to one oxygen atom
It is a mixture of hydrogen gas and oxygen gas
It contains twenty hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom

quiz.prompt: Which statement best describes the difference between a molecule and a compound?
quiz.answer: A compound needs two or more different elements; a molecule can be just one
quiz.explain: A molecule such as O2 can be a single element, but a compound like CO2 must combine at least two different elements.
choices: A molecule is held by weak forces, a compound by real chemical bonds
Every molecule counts as a compound, since any two joined atoms will do
A compound needs two or more different elements; a molecule can be just one
There is no real difference at all; the two words mean exactly the same thing

quiz.prompt: One molecule of glucose has the formula C6H12O6. How many atoms are there in a single glucose molecule altogether?
quiz.explain: 6 carbon + 12 hydrogen + 6 oxygen = 24 atoms in one molecule.

quiz.prompt: A candle burns away to almost nothing, giving off carbon dioxide and water vapour. What became of the atoms that were in the wax?
quiz.answer: They were rearranged into new molecules
choices: They were rearranged into new molecules
They were destroyed, which is why the wax vanished
New atoms were created for the gases
They shrank until they were light enough to float off
quiz.explain: Burning rearranges atoms; it does not make or destroy them. Weigh the gases and they account for the missing wax.

quiz.prompt: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a deadly poison, but carbon dioxide (CO2) is the gas that makes drinks fizzy. Both are built from carbon and oxygen alone. Why are they so different?
quiz.answer: One carbon holds one oxygen, the other holds two
choices: They are really one substance that goes by two different names
The carbon in the poison came from a more dangerous element
One of them is a mixture and the other one is a compound
One carbon holds one oxygen, the other holds two
quiz.explain: The other holds two, so they are different compounds. Change how many atoms of each element join, and you get a different compound. The atoms are the same; the recipe is not.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a molecule but NOT a compound?
quiz.answer: O2, two oxygen atoms bonded together
choices: H2O, hydrogen bonded to oxygen
CO2, carbon bonded to two oxygens
O2, two oxygen atoms bonded together
NaCl, sodium bonded tightly to chlorine
quiz.explain: A molecule is two or more atoms bonded together. It only counts as a compound if those atoms come from different elements, and O2 is oxygen twice over.

quiz.prompt: Sulfuric acid has the formula H2SO4. How many atoms are there in one molecule of it?
quiz.explain: 2 hydrogen + 1 sulfur + 4 oxygen = 7 atoms.

quiz.prompt: Ammonia has the formula NH3. How many hydrogen atoms are there in 4 ammonia molecules?
quiz.explain: 3 hydrogens per molecule, and 4 x 3 = 12.

quiz.prompt: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) bleaches hair, while water (H2O) does not, although both hold only hydrogen and oxygen. What does that show?
quiz.answer: How many atoms of each element the formula has decides what the substance is.
choices: How many atoms of each element the formula has decides what the substance is.
Peroxide holds heavier versions of the same two atoms.
Peroxide is simply water with extra oxygen dissolved into it.
The two are really the same substance at different strengths.
quiz.explain: Change the number of atoms joined together and you have a different compound with different properties.

quiz.prompt: A student writes that oxygen gas, O2, is a compound. How should you correct that?
quiz.answer: Both its atoms come from one element, so it is not a compound.
choices: Both its atoms come from one element, so it is not a compound.
It counts as a compound, since two atoms have joined up.
It counts as a compound only while it is dissolved in water.
It is neither a molecule nor a compound, but a mixture.
quiz.explain: O2 is a molecule of an element. A compound needs two or more different elements chemically joined.

nodes.title: Mixtures and Solutions
nodes.goal: Separate mixtures; understand solutions.

quiz.prompt: You have a beaker of salty water and want to get the pure salt back. Which method works best?
quiz.answer: Evaporate or boil the water away, leaving the salt behind
quiz.explain: Dissolved salt does not settle out and will not stay behind on a filter, and pouring off the liquid takes the salt with it. Evaporating the water leaves the solid salt.
choices: Pour the clear liquid off the top and keep what is left behind
Let it stand until the salt sinks back to the bottom of the beaker
Evaporate or boil the water away, leaving the salt behind
Pour it through filter paper to catch the grains of salt

quiz.prompt: A mixture of sand and water is poured through filter paper. What happens?
quiz.answer: The sand is trapped on the paper and the water passes through
quiz.explain: Sand does not dissolve and its grains are too big to pass through the filter, so it stays while water flows through.
choices: The water is trapped on the paper and the sand passes through
Both the sand and water pass through unchanged
The sand is trapped on the paper and the water passes through
The sand dissolves and passes through with the water

quiz.prompt: You stir 5 grams of sugar into 95 grams of water and every grain dissolves. What is the mass of the sugary water, in grams?
quiz.explain: Dissolving hides the sugar but does not destroy it: 95 + 5 = 100 g. The balance proves the sugar is still there.

quiz.prompt: Two glasses look identical: one holds salty water, the other pure water. Which test would tell them apart, without tasting either?
quiz.answer: Boil a spoonful dry and look for white solid
choices: Boil a spoonful dry and look for white solid
Feel which glass is the colder one
Pour each through filter paper and see which one comes through
Look closely for cloudiness, since dissolved salt turns water milky
quiz.explain: Dissolved salt slips through filter paper, salty water looks perfectly clear, and both glasses have long since come to room temperature. Boiling the water off leaves the salt behind.

quiz.prompt: A jar holds iron filings mixed into dry sand. Which method separates the two quickest?
quiz.answer: Run a magnet through it to lift the iron out
choices: Run a magnet through it to lift the iron out
Add water and pour it all through filter paper
Sieve the mixture to catch the larger iron filings
Stir hard so the lighter iron floats up to the top
quiz.explain: Iron is magnetic and sand is not, so a magnet lifts the filings straight out. Filtering catches both, sieving needs a size difference that is not there, and iron is the denser of the two.

quiz.prompt: Air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen and other gases. Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. What is the key difference between a mixture and a compound?
quiz.answer: In a compound the elements make a new substance; in a mixture they keep their own
choices: In a mixture the ingredients merely touch, while in a compound they dissolve into each other
A compound can be sieved apart, while a mixture must be boiled
A mixture holds more than two ingredients, a compound exactly two
In a compound the elements make a new substance; in a mixture they keep their own
quiz.explain: Oxygen in air still behaves like oxygen. Oxygen locked into water does not: hydrogen and oxygen have made something new.

quiz.prompt: You dissolve 12 grams of salt in 188 grams of water and it all disappears. What is the mass of the solution, in grams?
quiz.explain: Nothing is lost on dissolving, so 12 + 188 = 200 g.

quiz.prompt: A solution contains 20 grams of sugar dissolved in 80 grams of water. What percentage of the solution's mass is sugar?
quiz.explain: 20 out of a total 100 grams is 20 percent.

quiz.prompt: A muddy river sample is left standing until the silt settles, then the clear water is poured carefully off the top. What is this method called?
quiz.answer: Decanting.
choices: Decanting.
Distillation.
Chromatography.
Filtration.
quiz.explain: Decanting simply pours the liquid off a settled solid; no filter or heating is involved.

quiz.prompt: You need to recover both the pure water and the salt from a beaker of seawater. Which method gives you both?
quiz.answer: Distillation, collecting the condensed water and keeping the solid left behind.
choices: Distillation, collecting the condensed water and keeping the solid left behind.
Boiling in an open pan until all the water has gone.
Filtering the seawater through fine filter paper.
Freezing the seawater and pouring the liquid away.
quiz.explain: Distillation evaporates the water and then condenses it back, so both parts of the mixture are saved.

nodes.title: Chemical Reactions
nodes.goal: Signs that a new substance has formed.

quiz.prompt: You mix two clear liquids and a solid cloudy powder suddenly appears at the bottom, and the beaker gets warm. What is the best conclusion?
quiz.answer: A chemical reaction happened, forming a new substance
quiz.explain: A new solid forming plus a temperature change are classic signs that new substances were made in a chemical reaction.
choices: Nothing chemical happened; the liquids just got dirty
Only a physical change: the powder was there all along and has settled
The two liquids only changed color but stayed the same substances
A chemical reaction happened, forming a new substance

quiz.prompt: Which of these is NOT a reliable sign that a chemical reaction has taken place?
quiz.answer: An ice cube slowly melting into liquid water
quiz.explain: Melting is only a physical change of state; the water is still water, so no new substance formed.
choices: Heat or light being given off
Bubbles of gas fizzing up from a mixture
An ice cube slowly melting into liquid water
A permanent color change that will not reverse

quiz.prompt: A sealed flask holding 40 grams of vinegar and 5 grams of baking soda is placed on a balance. The mixture fizzes hard inside the sealed flask. What does the balance read afterwards, in grams?
quiz.explain: Nothing can leave a sealed flask, so the mass stays 40 + 5 = 45 g. Reactions rearrange atoms; they never lose them.

quiz.prompt: The same reaction is run in an open cup. 40 grams of vinegar and 5 grams of baking soda fizz away, and afterwards the cup and its contents weigh only 43 grams. Where did the other 2 grams go?
quiz.answer: It escaped as carbon dioxide gas, which has mass
choices: It escaped as carbon dioxide gas, which has mass
Some of the liquid turned into energy and left as heat
The vinegar soaked its way into the sides of the paper cup
Mass was destroyed by the chemical reaction that took place
quiz.explain: The bubbles carried carbon dioxide out of the open cup. Catch that gas and the missing 2 g turns up again.

quiz.prompt: Which pair contains two chemical changes?
quiz.answer: Toasting bread and rusting iron
choices: Boiling water and rusting iron
Toasting bread and rusting iron
Crushing chalk and freezing juice
Melting butter and dissolving sugar
quiz.explain: Toast and rust are new substances that will not go back. Boiling, crushing, freezing, melting and dissolving all leave the substance itself unchanged.

quiz.prompt: Iron wool is weighed, burned in air, and the grey powder left behind weighs MORE than the wool did. A student insists that burning makes things lighter, the way a log turns to ash. What is the best explanation?
quiz.answer: Oxygen from the air joined the iron, adding its mass to the powder
choices: The balance must be faulty, because burning takes mass away
Heat has a mass of its own, and the powder soaked some up
The iron swelled up as it burned, and bigger things weigh more
Oxygen from the air joined the iron, adding its mass to the powder
quiz.explain: Burning iron is iron combining with oxygen. A log seems to lose mass only because its gases drift away unweighed.

quiz.prompt: 6 grams of magnesium burns with 4 grams of oxygen and forms magnesium oxide. What mass of magnesium oxide, in grams, is made?
quiz.explain: Mass is conserved, so 6 + 4 = 10 grams of product.

quiz.prompt: 16 grams of methane burns with 64 grams of oxygen, giving 44 grams of carbon dioxide plus water. What mass of water, in grams, is made?
quiz.explain: Total mass in is 80 g, and 80 - 44 = 36 g of water.

quiz.prompt: A cut apple turns brown on the bench over an hour. Which observation best supports calling this a chemical change?
quiz.answer: A new brown substance has formed and will not turn back.
choices: A new brown substance has formed and will not turn back.
The apple has gone softer to the touch.
The apple has lost water and shrunk a little.
The apple's smell has grown slightly stronger.
quiz.explain: The test for a chemical change is a new substance that is not easily reversed; softening and drying are physical changes.

quiz.prompt: A burning candle is covered with a sealed jar and goes out after a minute. Which explanation fits?
quiz.answer: The oxygen inside the jar has been used up.
choices: The oxygen inside the jar has been used up.
The wax has run out of energy to give.
The glass of the jar has cooled the flame down.
The wax stopped melting the moment the jar went on.
quiz.explain: Burning needs a fuel and oxygen; sealing the jar limits the oxygen, and once it is used up the reaction stops.

nodes.title: Acids and Bases
nodes.goal: Sour, bitter, and the pH scale.

quiz.prompt: On the pH scale from 0 to 14, lemon juice has a pH of about 2 and soapy water has a pH of about 10. What does this tell you?
quiz.answer: Lemon juice is acidic and soapy water is basic
quiz.explain: A pH below 7 is acidic and a pH above 7 is basic, so lemon juice (2) is an acid and soapy water (10) is a base.
choices: Both are neutral because neither is exactly 7
Lemon juice is acidic and soapy water is basic
Both are acids because both have a pH below 14
Lemon juice is basic and soapy water is acidic

quiz.prompt: Pure water has a pH of 7. What does a pH of exactly 7 mean?
quiz.answer: The substance is neutral, neither acidic nor basic
quiz.explain: pH 7 sits at the middle of the scale and marks a neutral substance like pure water. Neutral does not mean empty: pure water still has acid and base particles, in equal numbers.
choices: The substance is a strong base, like oven cleaner
The substance holds neither any acid nor any base at all
The substance is neutral, neither acidic nor basic
The substance is a strong acid, like stomach acid

quiz.prompt: A student measures four liquids and records pH values of 3, 7, 9 and 13. How many of the four are basic?
quiz.explain: Basic means above 7, so the pH 9 and pH 13 liquids count. pH 3 is acidic and pH 7 is neutral.

quiz.prompt: Stomach acid has a pH of about 2; vinegar has a pH of about 3. Which one is the stronger acid?
quiz.answer: The stomach acid, because a lower pH always means more acidic
choices: They differ by only one pH unit, so the gap is too small to matter
The stomach acid, because a lower pH always means more acidic
The vinegar, because the bigger the number, the stronger the acid
They are equally acidic, since both sit below the neutral point of 7
quiz.explain: The pH scale runs backwards from what you might expect: the smaller the number, the more acidic the liquid. And each unit is a tenfold step, so one unit is a big gap.

quiz.prompt: You add exactly enough base to an acid to cancel it out. What have you made?
quiz.answer: A salt and water, sitting close to neutral
choices: A salt and water, sitting close to neutral
A stronger acid, since two chemicals combined
Pure water only, since the acid and base cancel out
A gas that fizzes off, leaving the beaker empty
quiz.explain: Acid plus base gives a salt plus water. The salt stays dissolved, so the beaker does not simply hold water. That is why indigestion tablets, which are bases, settle an acid stomach.

quiz.prompt: A gardener finds the soil too acidic for the plants to grow. What should be dug into it?
quiz.answer: Powdered lime, a base that cancels the acid
choices: Powdered lime, a base that cancels the acid
Vinegar, which is a weak acid
More fertiliser, since acid soil must be short of nutrients
Extra rainwater, which is slightly acidic itself
quiz.explain: A base neutralises acid, so lime raises the soil pH. Vinegar and rainwater are acidic and would make matters worse, and fertiliser adds nutrients without touching the pH.

quiz.prompt: Four liquids are measured and give pH values of 1, 4, 7 and 11. How many of the four are acidic?
quiz.explain: Below pH 7 counts as acidic, so pH 1 and pH 4: two of them.

quiz.prompt: Lemon juice has a pH of about 2 and milk a pH of about 6. By how many pH units do they differ?
quiz.explain: 6 - 2 = 4 pH units.

quiz.prompt: Indigestion tablets ease a burning stomach. What are they doing chemically?
quiz.answer: Neutralising some of the stomach's acid with a base.
choices: Neutralising some of the stomach's acid with a base.
Diluting the acid by adding water to the stomach.
Coating the stomach so it stops making any juices.
Turning the acid into a gas that is carried away.
quiz.explain: Antacids contain bases such as carbonates, which react with excess stomach acid and raise the pH towards neutral.

quiz.prompt: Red cabbage juice turns pink in one liquid and green in another. What is it being used as?
quiz.answer: An indicator.
choices: An indicator.
A neutraliser.
A catalyst.
A salt.
quiz.explain: An indicator is a substance that changes colour with pH; red cabbage juice is a natural one.

nodes.title: Reading the Periodic Table
nodes.goal: Groups, periods, metals and non-metals.

quiz.prompt: In the periodic table, what do the elements in the same vertical column (group) tend to share?
quiz.answer: Similar chemical behavior in reactions
quiz.explain: Elements in a group have the same number of outer electrons, which gives them similar chemical properties.
choices: The same number of protons in every atom
The same total atomic mass per atom
The same color, hardness, and texture
Similar chemical behavior in reactions

quiz.prompt: Most elements on the left and center of the periodic table are metals. Which set of properties is typical of a metal?
quiz.answer: Shiny, conducts electricity, and bends without breaking
quiz.explain: Metals are typically lustrous, malleable, and good conductors of heat and electricity. Only a few of them are magnetic, and a metal conducts as a solid as well as a liquid.
choices: Shiny and dense, but unable to conduct until it is molten
Magnetic in every case, and a good conductor of electricity
Dull, brittle, and a very poor conductor of electricity
Shiny, conducts electricity, and bends without breaking

quiz.prompt: The elements are lined up in order of how many protons their atoms hold. Chlorine is element number 17. How many protons has an atom of the element sitting immediately before chlorine?
quiz.explain: Each step back along the table removes one proton, so the element before chlorine (17) has 16, which is sulfur.

quiz.prompt: Sodium sits in group 1 and fizzes violently on water. Potassium sits directly below sodium in the same group. What should you predict when potassium meets water?
quiz.answer: It reacts violently too, since a group behaves alike
choices: It reacts violently too, since a group behaves alike
It sits there quietly, because it is heavier than sodium
It reacts the same way, but only if the water is warmed first
It reacts more gently than sodium, because it sits lower down
quiz.explain: Group members share an outer-electron count, so they react in the same way. Potassium is in fact even more violent than sodium: in group 1 reactivity grows going down.

quiz.prompt: Helium, neon and argon fill the last column of the table and take almost no part in reactions. What is this family called?
quiz.answer: The noble gases
choices: The halogens
The noble gases
The alkali metals
The transition metals
quiz.explain: Their outer shells are already full, so they have no reason to swap or share electrons. That is why they sit out of reactions.

quiz.prompt: A newly made element turns out to be a dull, brittle solid that does not carry electricity. Where in the periodic table would you expect it to sit?
quiz.answer: On the right, among the non-metals
choices: On the right, among the non-metals
Right at the bottom of the table
On the far left, among the reactive metals
In the middle block, among the transition metals
quiz.explain: Dull, brittle and non-conducting are the classic non-metal properties, and the non-metals are gathered on the right of the table.

quiz.prompt: Potassium is element number 19, and its most common atoms have a mass number of 39. How many neutrons are in one such nucleus?
quiz.explain: 39 - 19 = 20 neutrons.

quiz.prompt: Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon fill the final column of the table. How many elements is that?
quiz.explain: Counting them gives 6 elements in that group.

quiz.prompt: Fluorine and chlorine both sit in group 7 and both react with sodium to make a white salt. What does that show?
quiz.answer: Elements in the same group behave alike.
choices: Elements in the same group behave alike.
Elements react alike when they weigh the same.
Fluorine and chlorine are really the same element.
Salt can be made by joining up any two elements.
quiz.explain: A group shares an outer-shell arrangement, which is what sets its chemical behaviour.

quiz.prompt: A new element is made a few atoms at a time and placed at the far right-hand end of the last row. What behaviour would chemists expect from it?
quiz.answer: Very little reaction, in keeping with the noble gases above it.
choices: Very little reaction, in keeping with the noble gases above it.
Violent reaction with water, like the metals on the far left.
Snapping up electrons from metals, like the group 7 elements beside it.
Strong magnetism, like the metals in the middle block.
quiz.explain: Position predicts properties: the far right-hand column is the noble gases, which are famously unreactive. The reactive non-metals sit one column to their left.

nodes.title: Atomic Structure
nodes.goal: Protons, neutrons, electrons and electron shells.

quiz.prompt: A neutral atom of aluminum has 13 protons and a mass number of 27. How many neutrons are in its nucleus?
quiz.explain: Neutrons = mass number minus protons = 27 - 13 = 14.

quiz.prompt: Two atoms both have 6 protons, but one has 6 neutrons and the other has 8 neutrons. What is their relationship?
quiz.answer: They are isotopes of the same element, carbon
quiz.explain: The proton number (6) defines the element as carbon; differing neutron counts make them isotopes. Allotropes differ in how atoms are arranged, not in what the atoms are.
choices: They are isotopes of the same element, carbon
They are allotropes, two forms of carbon like diamond and graphite
They are ions of oxygen with different charges
They are two completely different elements

quiz.prompt: A neutral magnesium atom holds twelve electrons. Shells fill in the order two, then eight, then the remainder. How many electrons end up in the outermost occupied shell?
quiz.explain: Filling two in the first shell and eight in the second uses ten, leaving two electrons in the third shell.

quiz.prompt: A chloride ion, Cl-, forms when a neutral chlorine atom of 17 protons gains one electron. How many electrons does the chloride ion carry?
quiz.explain: The neutral atom has 17 electrons to match its 17 protons; gaining one more gives 18, which is why the ion carries a single negative charge.

quiz.prompt: Chlorine's relative atomic mass is quoted as 35.5, yet no single chlorine atom weighs 35.5 units. How can both statements be true?
quiz.answer: An average over isotopes: about three chlorine-35 atoms for each chlorine-37
choices: It averages masses 35 and 37, which occur in equal numbers of atoms
The half unit comes from the mass of the orbiting electrons
An average over isotopes: about three chlorine-35 atoms for each chlorine-37
Chlorine atoms gain and lose mass constantly as they move about
quiz.explain: A three-to-one mix of masses 35 and 37 averages to 35.5; an equal mix would have averaged 36. Relative atomic mass describes a sample, not any one atom.

quiz.prompt: Rutherford fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Almost all sailed straight through, but roughly one in eight thousand bounced sharply back toward the source. What does that rare bounce show?
quiz.answer: A tiny, dense, positively charged core sits at the centre
choices: Positive charge is spread evenly through the whole atom
The nucleus must be big enough to block one alpha in eight thousand
A tiny, dense, positively charged core sits at the centre
Electrons in orbit are heavy enough to turn the alphas back
quiz.explain: Only a small, massive, strongly positive target could repel a fast alpha particle straight back. The rarity of the bounce is what shows the core is tiny, not that it is large.

quiz.prompt: An Fe3+ ion is formed from an iron atom with 26 protons. How many electrons does the ion hold?
quiz.explain: 26 protons minus a 3+ charge means 26 - 3 = 23 electrons.

quiz.prompt: Copper is 69 percent copper-63 and 31 percent copper-65. What is its relative atomic mass, to one decimal place?
A neon sample gives mass-spectrometer peaks at 20 and 22 in a ratio of about nine to one. What does that tell you?
quiz.answer: Neon has two isotopes with different numbers of neutrons.
choices: Neon has two isotopes with different numbers of neutrons.
Neon atoms gain mass when they are ionised in the machine.
The sample is contaminated with a heavier element.
Some of the neon atoms have picked up two extra protons.
quiz.explain: Same element, different neutron counts: the peak positions give the mass numbers and the heights give the abundances.

quiz.prompt: A student pictures electrons orbiting like planets at fixed distances and concludes an atom must be mostly solid. Diagnose the error.
quiz.answer: An atom is mostly empty space, and electrons occupy fuzzy clouds, not tracks.
choices: An atom is mostly empty space, and electrons occupy fuzzy clouds, not tracks.
Electrons do orbit like planets, only far more slowly.
The electrons' orbits are packed so tightly that they fill the atom.
The nucleus fills the atom and the electrons sit on its surface.
quiz.explain: Rutherford's scattering showed the nucleus is tiny compared with the atom, and quantum mechanics replaced orbits with orbitals.

nodes.title: Chemical Bonding
nodes.goal: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonds.

quiz.prompt: Sodium (a metal) reacts with chlorine (a non-metal) to form table salt. What kind of bond forms and why?
quiz.answer: Ionic, because sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, forming ions
quiz.explain: A metal donating electrons to a non-metal produces charged ions held together by ionic attraction.
choices: No bond forms; salt is only a physical mixture of the two elements
Metallic, because both atoms release their electrons into a shared sea
Covalent, because the two atoms share a pair of electrons equally
Ionic, because sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, forming ions

quiz.prompt: Two chlorine atoms bond to form Cl2 gas. What type of bond holds them together?
quiz.answer: A covalent bond in which the atoms share electrons
quiz.explain: Two identical non-metal atoms share electrons equally, which is a covalent bond.
choices: A covalent bond in which the atoms share electrons
An ionic bond with one atom taking electrons from the other
A metallic bond with delocalized electrons
A hydrogen bond between the two atoms

quiz.prompt: A shiny piece of copper conducts electricity and can be bent into wire without shattering. Which bonding model best explains these properties?
quiz.answer: Metallic bonding, with positive ions in a sea of mobile electrons
quiz.explain: Free-moving delocalized electrons carry current, and the sliding lattice lets metals bend rather than crack.
choices: Metallic bonding, with electrons fixed on each atom and ions free to slide
Metallic bonding, with positive ions in a sea of mobile electrons
Covalent bonding, with fixed shared pairs between neighboring atoms
Ionic bonding, with rigid alternating positive and negative ions

quiz.prompt: Magnesium loses two electrons to form Mg(2+), and chlorine gains one to form Cl-. In the compound they build, how many chloride ions balance each magnesium ion?
quiz.explain: The charges must cancel: one Mg(2+) needs two Cl- ions, giving MgCl2.

quiz.prompt: Sodium chloride melts at 801 degrees Celsius; chlorine, Cl2, melts at -101 degrees Celsius. Both contain chlorine. Why is the gap so enormous?
quiz.answer: Melting NaCl breaks a whole ionic lattice; melting Cl2 only parts molecule from molecule
choices: Sodium chloride molecules are much heavier than chlorine molecules
Chlorine is a gas, and gases have no bonds holding them together
The covalent bonds inside Cl2 are weaker than ionic bonds, so they snap at a lower temperature
Melting NaCl breaks a whole ionic lattice; melting Cl2 only parts molecule from molecule
quiz.explain: Melting Cl2 never breaks the Cl-Cl bond; it only separates one molecule from the next. Melting NaCl has to break up the whole ionic lattice.

quiz.prompt: Solid sodium chloride will not carry a current, but molten sodium chloride conducts well. What has changed on melting?
quiz.answer: The ions are freed from the lattice and can drift
choices: The ions are freed from the lattice and can drift
Melting turns the solid into a solution, and solutions always conduct
Melting shakes electrons loose from the sodium to carry current
Charged NaCl molecules form in the liquid and move to the electrodes
quiz.explain: Charge is carried by ions that can move. In the solid they are locked in a lattice; in the melt they are free to travel to the electrodes.

quiz.prompt: Calcium forms Ca2+ ions and nitrogen forms N3- ions. How many calcium ions are needed to balance two nitride ions?
quiz.explain: Two N3- carry 6 negative charges, and 3 Ca2+ carry 6 positive: the formula is Ca3N2.

quiz.prompt: In a molecule of methane, CH4, how many bonding pairs of electrons surround the carbon atom?
quiz.explain: Carbon forms four single bonds, so four bonding pairs.

quiz.prompt: Iodine melts at only 114 degrees Celsius and sublimes readily, even though the bond inside each I2 molecule is strong. What explains the low melting point?
quiz.answer: Only weak forces act between the molecules.
choices: Only weak forces act between the molecules.
The covalent bonds inside the molecules are being broken.
Iodine forms a lattice of ions that is held together loosely.
Iodine molecules repel one another electrically.
quiz.explain: Melting a molecular solid separates whole molecules, overcoming weak intermolecular forces, not the strong covalent bonds within them.

quiz.prompt: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon, yet graphite conducts electricity along its layers and diamond does not. Explain the difference.
quiz.answer: One electron per carbon stays free in graphite; in diamond all four are bonded.
choices: Graphite contains metallic impurities that carry the current.
One electron per carbon stays free in graphite; in diamond all four are bonded.
Graphite's atoms are ionised, so its ions carry the charge.
Diamond's bonds are ionic, and a solid ionic lattice cannot carry a current.
quiz.explain: Structure decides properties: graphite's delocalised electrons conduct; diamond's fully bonded tetrahedral network has none free.

nodes.title: Moles and Equations
nodes.goal: Balance equations; count with the mole.

quiz.prompt: Balance the equation for the combustion of methane: CH4 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O. What is the coefficient in front of O2 when the equation is correctly balanced with whole numbers?
quiz.explain: CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O balances 1 C, 4 H, and 4 O on each side.

quiz.prompt: How many moles of water molecules are in a sample containing 3.011 x 10^24 water molecules? (Avogadro's number is 6.022 x 10^23 per mole.)
The molar mass of water (H2O) is 18 g/mol. What is the mass, in grams, of 2 moles of water?
quiz.explain: Mass = moles x molar mass = 2 mol x 18 g/mol = 36 g.

quiz.prompt: Aluminium burns according to 4 Al + 3 O2 -> 2 Al2O3. If 8 moles of aluminium react completely, how many moles of Al2O3 form?
quiz.explain: The equation gives 2 Al2O3 for every 4 Al, a 1:2 ratio, so 8 moles of Al yield 4 moles of Al2O3.

quiz.prompt: Asked to balance H2 + O2 -> H2O, a student writes H2 + O2 -> H2O2 and says the atoms now match. What is wrong with that fix?
quiz.answer: Changing a formula makes a different substance; only coefficients may change
choices: Nothing is wrong: the atoms do balance now, so the equation is correct
The formula is fine, since H2O2 and H2O are the same substance
Changing a formula makes a different substance; only coefficients may change
Oxygen has to be written as a single O atom inside equations
quiz.explain: H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide, not water. Balance by adjusting coefficients: 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O.

quiz.prompt: Heating limestone drives off carbon dioxide: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. The molar mass of CaCO3 is 100 g/mol. How many moles of CO2 come off 50 grams of calcium carbonate?
quiz.explain: 50 g / 100 g per mol = 0.5 mol of CaCO3, and the 1:1 ratio gives 0.5 mol of CO2.

quiz.prompt: Carbon dioxide has a molar mass of 44 g/mol. What is the mass, in grams, of 0.25 mol of it?
For 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O, how many moles of water form from 5 moles of hydrogen with oxygen in excess?
quiz.explain: Hydrogen and water appear in a 2:2 ratio, so 5 mol of H2 gives 5 mol of water.

quiz.prompt: A reaction should give 8.0 grams of product but only 6.0 grams is collected. What is the percentage yield?
quiz.explain: 6.0 / 8.0 = 0.75, which is a 75 percent yield.

quiz.prompt: A plant runs N2 + 3 H2 -> 2 NH3 with 1 mol of nitrogen and 2 mol of hydrogen, and expects 2 mol of ammonia. What actually limits the yield?
quiz.answer: Hydrogen runs out first, capping the ammonia near 1.33 mol.
choices: Hydrogen runs out first, capping the ammonia near 1.33 mol.
Nitrogen runs out first, capping the ammonia at 1 mol.
Neither runs out, so the full 2 mol of ammonia is made.
Both run out together, giving exactly 2 mol of ammonia.
quiz.explain: Three moles of hydrogen are needed per mole of nitrogen; with only 2 mol of hydrogen it is the limiting reactant, giving 2 x 2/3 mol of ammonia.

nodes.title: Types of Reactions
nodes.goal: Redox, acid-base, precipitation.

quiz.prompt: In the reaction Zn + Cu(2+) -> Zn(2+) + Cu, what is happening to the zinc atom?
quiz.answer: It is being oxidized, losing electrons
quiz.explain: Zinc goes from 0 to +2, losing two electrons, which is oxidation.
choices: It is being oxidized, losing electrons
It is displacing copper with no change in oxidation state
It is dissolving physically, with no electrons moving at all
It is being reduced, gaining electrons

quiz.prompt: Mixing solutions of silver nitrate and sodium chloride produces a cloudy white solid of silver chloride. What type of reaction is this?
quiz.answer: A precipitation reaction
quiz.explain: Two soluble salts swap partners to form an insoluble solid (a precipitate), the hallmark of a precipitation reaction.
choices: A combustion reaction
A precipitation reaction
An acid-base neutralization
A single-displacement redox reaction

quiz.prompt: Hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide to give sodium chloride and water. This is best classified as which type of reaction?
quiz.answer: Acid-base neutralization, giving a salt and water
quiz.explain: An acid and a base combining to yield a salt plus water is a neutralization reaction, with no change in oxidation states.
choices: Precipitation, because a solid forms
Combustion, because heat is released
Redox, because electrons are transferred
Acid-base neutralization, giving a salt and water

quiz.prompt: Balance the displacement reaction 2 Al + 3 CuSO4 -> Al2(SO4)3 + Cu. What coefficient belongs in front of the copper?
quiz.explain: Three copper ions are released by 3 CuSO4, so 3 Cu atoms are deposited: 2 Al + 3 CuSO4 -> Al2(SO4)3 + 3 Cu.

quiz.prompt: A zinc strip is dropped into blue copper(II) sulfate solution. The blue fades and a red-brown deposit grows on the strip. Say what is transferred and in which direction, and state which species is reduced.
quiz.answer: Zinc atoms hand electrons to the copper(II) ions: the zinc is oxidised to Zn2+, and the copper ions are reduced to copper metal that plates onto the strip.
quiz.explain: Electrons flow from the more reactive metal to the ions of the less reactive one. Losing them is oxidation; the copper(II) ions gain them and are reduced.

quiz.prompt: Zinc dropped into copper(II) sulfate coats itself in copper. A student tries silver in copper(II) nitrate and sees nothing happen at all. Why not?
quiz.answer: Silver is less reactive than copper
choices: The solution was too dilute for a reaction to get going
Silver reacts with acids rather than with dissolved salts
A reaction did happen, but silver and copper look alike
Silver is less reactive than copper
quiz.explain: So it cannot displace copper from solution. Displacement runs one way only: a metal pushes out a less reactive one. Silver sits below copper in the reactivity series, so nothing happens.

quiz.prompt: In the permanganate ion MnO4-, each oxygen counts as -2. What is the oxidation number of the manganese? Give it as a positive number.
quiz.explain: Four oxygens give -8; for an overall -1 the manganese must be +7.

quiz.prompt: Balance the equation __ Fe + 3 Cl2 -> 2 FeCl3. What coefficient belongs in front of the iron?
quiz.explain: Two FeCl3 contain two iron atoms, so 2 Fe are needed.

quiz.prompt: Adding barium chloride solution to an unknown solution gives a white solid that will not dissolve in dilute acid. Which ion was present?
quiz.answer: Sulfate.
choices: Sulfate.
Carbonate.
Chloride, which gives a white precipitate with barium.
Hydroxide, which gives a white gel instead.
quiz.explain: Barium sulfate is a white precipitate insoluble in acid; barium carbonate would dissolve with fizzing, and barium chloride is itself soluble.

quiz.prompt: A strip of copper is dropped into silver nitrate solution. The solution turns blue and silvery crystals grow on the copper. What has been oxidised and what reduced?
quiz.answer: Copper is oxidised and silver ions are reduced.
choices: Copper is oxidised and silver ions are reduced.
Silver is oxidised and copper ions are reduced.
Both the copper and the silver are oxidised at once.
Neither: this is a simple precipitation of silver.
quiz.explain: Copper atoms lose electrons to form blue Cu2+ ions, and silver ions gain those electrons to deposit as silver metal.

nodes.title: Gas Laws
nodes.goal: Pressure, volume, temperature and the ideal gas.

quiz.prompt: A sealed gas sample occupies 4.0 L at a pressure of 2.0 atm. At constant temperature, what volume in liters will it occupy if the pressure is lowered to 1.0 atm? (Use Boyle's law, P1V1 = P2V2.)
A balloon is taken from a warm room into a cold freezer at constant pressure. According to the gas laws, what happens to its volume?
quiz.answer: It shrinks, because volume decreases as temperature falls
quiz.explain: By Charles's law, at constant pressure gas volume is proportional to absolute temperature, so cooling shrinks the balloon. A rubber balloon cannot hold its size at a lower pressure.
choices: It stays exactly the same, because gas volume ignores temperature
It expands, because cold gas takes up more space
It shrinks, because volume decreases as temperature falls
It keeps its size, but the pressure inside it drops

quiz.prompt: Using the ideal gas law PV = nRT with R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K), what is the pressure in atm of 1.0 mol of gas in a 22.4 L container at 273 K? Round to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: P = nRT/V = (1.0 x 0.0821 x 273) / 22.4 = 1.0 atm, standard conditions.

quiz.prompt: A gas occupies 300 mL at 27 degrees Celsius. It is warmed to 327 degrees Celsius at constant pressure. Converting to kelvin first, what volume in mL does it now occupy?
quiz.explain: 27 C = 300 K and 327 C = 600 K, so the absolute temperature doubles and V2 = 300 x (600/300) = 600 mL.

quiz.prompt: A student predicts that a gas warmed from 20 to 40 degrees Celsius at constant pressure will double in volume, because the temperature doubled. Where does that reasoning fail?
quiz.answer: Volume tracks absolute temperature
choices: Charles's law holds at constant volume, not at constant pressure
Doubling temperature halves volume
Volume responds to pressure alone, so temperature does not matter
Volume tracks absolute temperature
quiz.explain: So 293 K to 313 K is a rise of only about 7 percent. Celsius has an arbitrary zero, so ratios in Celsius mean nothing. In kelvin the temperature rises by about 7 percent, and so does the volume.

quiz.prompt: A car tyre is inflated to 2.0 atm at 300 K. After a long drive the air inside reaches 330 K, with the volume unchanged. What is the new pressure, in atm?
quiz.explain: At constant volume P/T is constant, so P2 = 2.0 x (330/300) = 2.2 atm.

quiz.prompt: A gas occupies 2.5 L at 1.0 atm. At constant temperature, what volume in litres does it occupy at 0.50 atm?
quiz.explain: Boyle's law: halving the pressure doubles the volume, so 5.0 L.

quiz.prompt: Using PV = nRT with R = 0.0821 L atm per mol K, what volume in litres does 2.0 mol of gas occupy at 1.0 atm and 273 K? Give one decimal place.
A sealed rigid vessel of gas at 400 K is at 3.0 atm. It is cooled to 200 K at constant volume. What is the new pressure, in atm?
quiz.explain: Pressure is proportional to absolute temperature at fixed volume, so halving T halves P: 1.5 atm.

quiz.prompt: A sealed bag of crisps swells noticeably as it is carried up a mountain, although the temperature hardly changes. Explain what happened.
quiz.answer: The outside pressure has fallen.
choices: The outside pressure has fallen.
The gas was warmed by the climb.
Extra air has leaked into the bag on the way up.
The colder air outside has made the gas expand.
quiz.explain: At altitude the atmosphere pushes in less hard, so the trapped gas expands until the pressures balance again.

nodes.title: Energy in Reactions
nodes.goal: Exothermic, endothermic, and reaction rates.

quiz.prompt: When ammonium nitrate dissolves in water, the beaker feels noticeably colder. How is this reaction classified?
quiz.answer: Endothermic, because it absorbs heat from the surroundings
quiz.explain: The cooling shows heat is being drawn in from the water, which is endothermic.
choices: Neither, because dissolving is physical and transfers no heat
Exothermic, because it releases stored heat to the surroundings
Endothermic, because it absorbs heat from the surroundings
Exothermic, because breaking the ionic lattice gives out heat

quiz.prompt: You want a reaction to go faster. Which change will generally INCREASE the reaction rate?
quiz.answer: Raising the temperature so collisions are more frequent
quiz.explain: Higher temperature increases both the frequency and energy of collisions, speeding up the reaction.
choices: Diluting the reactants down to lower their concentration
Cooling the mixture so the molecules move more slowly
Raising the temperature so collisions are more frequent
Pressing a powdered solid reactant into one large lump

quiz.prompt: In an exothermic reaction, how does the energy of the products compare to the energy of the reactants?
quiz.answer: The products have lower energy, and the difference leaves as heat
quiz.explain: Exothermic reactions drop to lower-energy products, releasing the surplus energy as heat.
choices: The products have lower energy, and the difference leaves as heat
The products have higher energy, absorbed from the surroundings
The products have lower energy, but the reaction still absorbs heat
The products and the reactants end up with exactly equal energy

quiz.prompt: Breaking bonds takes energy in and making bonds gives energy out. A reaction absorbs 1500 kJ/mol breaking bonds and releases 1650 kJ/mol forming them. What is the overall energy change, in kJ/mol? Give a negative number if energy is released.
quiz.explain: Overall change = energy in - energy out = 1500 - 1650 = -150 kJ/mol, so the reaction is exothermic.

quiz.prompt: Two 5 gram samples of marble react with excess acid: one is a single chip, the other is ground to fine powder. How do the two runs compare?
quiz.answer: The powder fizzes faster but gives the same total volume of gas
choices: The powder fizzes faster and gives more gas in total
The powder reacts more slowly, since its pieces are smaller
Both react at the same rate, because the two masses are equal
The powder fizzes faster but gives the same total volume of gas
quiz.explain: Surface area sets the rate, not the amount. Equal masses of marble contain equal amounts of carbonate, so both release the same gas in the end.

quiz.prompt: Heating a mixture and adding a catalyst both make a reaction go faster. What does the catalyst do that heating does not?
quiz.answer: It opens a route with a lower activation energy
choices: It opens a route with a lower activation energy
It makes the reaction release more energy overall
It gives the colliding molecules more kinetic energy
It increases the number of reactant molecules present
quiz.explain: Heating pushes more molecules over the barrier; a catalyst lowers the barrier itself, so more collisions succeed even at the old temperature.

quiz.prompt: A reaction releases 250 kJ per mole. How many kilojoules are released when 0.40 mol reacts?
Breaking the bonds in a reaction takes in 2200 kJ/mol and forming the new bonds gives out 2500 kJ/mol. What is the enthalpy change, in kJ/mol?
quiz.explain: 2200 - 2500 = -300 kJ/mol: more energy out than in, so the reaction is exothermic.

quiz.prompt: Two identical marble chips react with excess acid, one at 20 degrees Celsius and one at 40 degrees Celsius. How do their graphs of gas volume against time compare?
quiz.answer: The warmer one climbs more steeply but levels off at the same volume.
choices: The warmer one climbs more steeply but levels off at the same volume.
The warmer one levels off at a higher final volume.
The two curves lie exactly on top of one another.
The warmer one climbs more steeply and never levels off.
quiz.explain: Temperature changes the rate, not the amount: the same mass of marble yields the same volume of carbon dioxide in the end.

quiz.prompt: A catalyst is added to a reversible reaction that has not yet reached equilibrium. What happens to the yield at equilibrium?
quiz.answer: It is unchanged; equilibrium simply arrives sooner.
choices: It is unchanged; equilibrium simply arrives sooner.
It rises, because the forward route has been favoured.
It falls, because the reverse route has sped up more.
It rises, but only when the reaction gives out heat.
quiz.explain: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both directions equally, so the equilibrium position is untouched and only the approach is faster.

nodes.title: Carbon Chemistry
nodes.goal: Why carbon builds the molecules of life.

quiz.prompt: Carbon is uniquely able to build the huge variety of molecules found in living things. What property of carbon makes this possible?
quiz.answer: Each carbon forms four stable bonds, building chains and rings
quiz.explain: Carbon's four bonds let it link into chains, branches, and rings, generating enormous molecular diversity. Silicon and sulfur also chain up, just far less readily, and carbon is nowhere near the most abundant element.
choices: Carbon is the only element able to bond to itself in long chains
Each carbon forms four stable bonds, building chains and rings
Carbon has six electrons, so it can bond to six neighbours at once
Carbon is the most abundant element on Earth, so there is most of it

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is a hydrocarbon?
quiz.answer: Methane, CH4
quiz.explain: A hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen, which describes methane (CH4).
choices: Water, H2O
Carbon dioxide, CO2
Methane, CH4
Sodium chloride, NaCl

quiz.prompt: In a molecule of ethane, each of the 2 carbon atoms forms 4 bonds total: one to the other carbon and the rest to hydrogen atoms. How many hydrogen atoms are in one ethane molecule?
quiz.explain: Each carbon bonds once to the other carbon and three times to hydrogen, giving 2 x 3 = 6 hydrogens (C2H6).

quiz.prompt: Alkanes follow the pattern CnH(2n+2): butane is C4H10 and pentane is C5H12. How many hydrogen atoms are in hexane, which has 6 carbons?
quiz.explain: 2n + 2 with n = 6 gives 2(6) + 2 = 14, so hexane is C6H14.

quiz.prompt: Diamond is the hardest natural material; candle wax dents under a fingernail. Both are built mostly from carbon atoms. What accounts for the difference?
quiz.answer: How the carbon atoms are bonded and arranged, rather than which element they are
choices: Diamond holds a heavier, harder kind of carbon atom
Wax is mostly hydrogen, and hydrogen makes a substance soft
Diamond formed under pressure, which hardened every atom permanently
How the carbon atoms are bonded and arranged, rather than which element they are
quiz.explain: Diamond is one rigid network of covalent bonds; wax is short chains that slide past each other. Same element, different architecture.

quiz.prompt: Ethene, C2H4, turns orange bromine water colourless within seconds. Ethane, C2H6, leaves it orange. What does the test reveal about ethene?
quiz.answer: It holds a carbon-carbon double bond
choices: It holds a carbon-carbon double bond
It bleaches the bromine by giving off a gas that destroys the colour
Bromine simply soaks into the gas
It simply dissolves the bromine and hides the orange colour
quiz.explain: Bromine adds across a double bond, so the orange colour disappears. Ethane has only single bonds and leaves the bromine untouched.

quiz.prompt: Propane has the formula C3H8. How many hydrogen atoms are there in 3 molecules of propane?
quiz.explain: 8 hydrogens per molecule, and 3 x 8 = 24.

quiz.prompt: Alkenes follow the pattern CnH2n. How many hydrogen atoms does an alkene with 7 carbon atoms hold?
quiz.explain: 2 x 7 = 14 hydrogen atoms.

quiz.prompt: Two liquids both have the formula C4H10 but boil at different temperatures. What accounts for that?
quiz.answer: They are isomers whose carbon skeletons are arranged differently.
choices: They are isomers whose carbon skeletons are arranged differently.
One sample is contaminated with a heavier alkane.
One contains heavier isotopes of carbon than the other.
A single formula cannot give two boiling points, so one was misread.
quiz.explain: Butane and methylpropane share a formula but differ in shape; the more branched molecule packs less well and boils lower.

quiz.prompt: A gas decolourises bromine water within seconds and burns with a smoky flame. Which family does it belong to?
quiz.answer: The alkenes.
choices: The alkenes.
The alkanes.
The alcohols, which also burn readily.
The carboxylic acids, which react with bromine.
quiz.explain: Rapid decolourising of bromine water is the standard test for a carbon-carbon double bond.

nodes.title: Physical Chemistry
nodes.goal: Thermodynamics and kinetics of chemical systems.

quiz.prompt: A reaction has a negative enthalpy change (ΔH < 0) and a positive entropy change (ΔS > 0). Using ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, what can you say about its spontaneity?
quiz.answer: It is spontaneous at all temperatures, since ΔG stays negative
quiz.explain: With ΔH negative and -TΔS also negative for all positive T, ΔG stays negative everywhere, so the reaction is always spontaneous.
choices: It is spontaneous only above a certain fairly high temperature
It is never spontaneous, however hot or cold the surroundings get
It is spontaneous at all temperatures, since ΔG stays negative
It is spontaneous only below a certain fairly low temperature

quiz.prompt: A reaction is endothermic (ΔH > 0) but has a large positive entropy change (ΔS > 0). Under what condition does it become spontaneous?
quiz.answer: At high temperature, where the TΔS term outweighs ΔH
quiz.explain: For positive ΔH and positive ΔS, ΔG = ΔH - TΔS turns negative once T is large enough.
choices: At no temperature at all, because ΔH is positive
At high temperature, where the TΔS term outweighs ΔH
At all temperatures, because a positive entropy change always wins
At low temperature, where the TΔS term stays small

quiz.prompt: Adding a catalyst to a reaction at equilibrium has what effect?
quiz.answer: It speeds both directions equally without shifting position
quiz.explain: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both directions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but K and the position are unchanged.
choices: It speeds both directions equally without shifting position
It shifts the equilibrium position across towards the products
It increases the final yield of the products at equilibrium
It raises the value of the equilibrium constant K itself

quiz.prompt: A reaction has ΔH = +40.0 kJ/mol and ΔS = +100 J/(mol·K), both roughly constant over the range of interest. Above what temperature, in kelvin, does it turn spontaneous?
quiz.explain: ΔG = 0 when T = ΔH/ΔS = 40000 J/mol ÷ 100 J/(mol·K) = 400 K. Above that, TΔS outweighs ΔH and ΔG goes negative.

quiz.prompt: A 1.00 L flask at equilibrium for H2 + I2 ⇌ 2 HI contains [H2] = 0.20 M, [I2] = 0.20 M and [HI] = 1.60 M. Calculate Kc.
The Haber process, N2 + 3 H2 ⇌ 2 NH3, gives out heat. A plant operator raises the temperature to speed things up and finds the equilibrium yield of ammonia has fallen. Choose the best account.
quiz.answer: Heat is a product here, so heating pushes the balance back and cuts yield
choices: Heating speeds the forward reaction alone, so the yield should have climbed
The catalyst lost activity at the higher temperature, so less ammonia formed
Temperature changes the rate but leaves the equilibrium constant fixed
Heat is a product here, so heating pushes the balance back and cuts yield
quiz.explain: Heat is a product of an exothermic reaction, so adding heat shifts the position back. A catalyst could not have changed the equilibrium yield either way. Industry accepts a lower yield to get a workable rate, then recycles.

quiz.prompt: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 20 minutes. After how many minutes does 12.5 percent of the reactant remain?
quiz.explain: 12.5 percent is one eighth, which is three half-lives: 3 x 20 = 60 minutes.

quiz.prompt: A reaction has enthalpy change -92 kJ/mol and entropy change -198 J/(mol K). Calculate the Gibbs energy change, in kJ/mol, at 298 K, to the nearest whole number.
A gas-phase equilibrium 2 A(g) is in balance with B(g). The vessel is compressed to half its volume at fixed temperature. Which way does the position shift?
quiz.answer: Towards B, the side with fewer gas molecules.
choices: Towards B, the side with fewer gas molecules.
Towards A, since compression favours the reactants.
Neither way, since both concentrations rise together.
Towards B, but only if the reaction gives out heat.
quiz.explain: Le Chatelier: raising the pressure pushes the system towards the side with the smaller number of gas molecules.

quiz.prompt: Doubling the concentration of A doubles a reaction's rate, and doubling the concentration of B quadruples it. What overall order does the rate law carry?
quiz.answer: Third order overall.
choices: Third order overall.
Second order overall.
First order in each, so second overall.
Fourth order, taking the larger of the two effects.
quiz.explain: Rate proportional to [A] to the first power and [B] squared gives an overall order of 1 + 2 = 3.

nodes.title: Organic Chemistry
nodes.goal: Functional groups, mechanisms, synthesis.

quiz.prompt: Ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) and ethanol (CH3CH2OH) are both colourless liquids. Stirring a spoonful of sodium carbonate into each makes only one of them fizz. Which one fizzes, and why?
quiz.answer: The ethanoic acid, because its -COOH group hands a proton to the carbonate
quiz.explain: A carboxyl group is acidic enough to protonate carbonate and release carbon dioxide. An alcohol's -OH is far too weak an acid to do that, even though it also carries O-H.
choices: The ethanol, because its -OH group is the more acidic of the two groups
The ethanoic acid, because its -COOH group hands a proton to the carbonate
Both of them, since each molecule ends in an oxygen bonded to a hydrogen
Neither of them, since carbonates fizz only with mineral acids such as HCl

quiz.prompt: An SN2 reaction is a single concerted step: the nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group. A chemist runs one on a single enantiomer of 2-bromobutane. Predict what the product looks like.
quiz.answer: One product, with the configuration at that carbon inverted
quiz.explain: Backside attack pushes the other three groups through like an umbrella in the wind, so a single enantiomer gives a single inverted product. A racemic mixture would point to a flat carbocation instead.
choices: A 50:50 mixture of the two configurations at that carbon
One product, with the configuration at that carbon inverted
One product, with the configuration at that carbon unchanged
A mixture of alkene and alcohol in roughly equal amounts

quiz.prompt: You need to oxidize a primary alcohol all the way to a carboxylic acid. Which reagent choice is appropriate?
quiz.answer: Acidified potassium dichromate heated under reflux
quiz.explain: A strong oxidant under reflux drives a primary alcohol past the aldehyde stage to the carboxylic acid. Distil instead and the aldehyde escapes before it can be oxidised further.
choices: Acidified potassium dichromate heated under reflux
Acidified dichromate, distilling the product off as it forms
A mild reducing agent such as sodium borohydride
Sodium hydroxide solution used on its own as a base

quiz.prompt: A hydrocarbon has the molecular formula C6H10. Using degrees of unsaturation = (2n + 2 − H) / 2 for n carbons, calculate its degrees of unsaturation.
quiz.explain: (2×6 + 2 − 10)/2 = (14 − 10)/2 = 2, so the molecule carries two rings or double bonds in some combination.

quiz.prompt: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts with water many times faster than 1-bromobutane under identical conditions. Account for the difference.
quiz.answer: The tertiary halide ionises to a carbocation stabilised by three alkyl groups
choices: The tertiary carbon-bromine bond is weaker, since more carbons pull on it
The tertiary halide follows SN2, which outruns SN1 in any solvent
Water reaches the tertiary carbon more easily, being the less crowded of the two
The tertiary halide ionises to a carbocation stabilised by three alkyl groups
quiz.explain: Rate-determining ionisation is easy for a tertiary substrate because alkyl groups stabilise the carbocation. Steric crowding actually blocks SN2 there.

quiz.prompt: An unknown liquid of formula C3H6O gives a strong infrared band at 1715 cm-1, no broad absorption near 3300 cm-1, and one single peak in its proton NMR. Identify it, with the reasoning.
quiz.answer: Propanone: a carbonyl with no O-H, and six equivalent hydrogens
choices: Propanal, since an aldehyde carbonyl absorbs there and would give a single NMR peak
Prop-2-en-1-ol, since its C=C accounts for the 1715 band and for the single peak
Propan-2-ol, since a missing broad band rules out acids rather than alcohols
Propanone: a carbonyl with no O-H, and six equivalent hydrogens
quiz.explain: Propanal would show three proton environments, and both alcohols would show a broad O-H stretch. Only propanone puts all six hydrogens in one environment.

quiz.prompt: A compound has the molecular formula C7H8. Using degrees of unsaturation = (2n + 2 - H)/2, how many degrees of unsaturation does it have?
quiz.explain: (2 x 7 + 2 - 8)/2 = (16 - 8)/2 = 4, consistent with a benzene ring plus its side chain.

quiz.prompt: How many structural isomers exist with the molecular formula C5H12?
quiz.explain: Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane: three isomers.

quiz.prompt: An unknown liquid shows a broad infrared band near 3000 to 3300 cm-1, a strong band at 1710 cm-1, and a molecular ion at m/z 60. Which compound fits?
quiz.answer: Ethanoic acid.
choices: Ethanoic acid.
Propan-1-ol.
Propanone.
Methyl methanoate, which also has mass 60.
quiz.explain: Mass 60 with both a broad O-H band and a carbonyl band points to a carboxylic acid; the ester and the ketone lack the broad O-H, and the alcohol lacks the 1710 band.

quiz.prompt: Warming 1-bromopropane with aqueous sodium hydroxide gives an alcohol, but with sodium hydroxide dissolved in ethanol it gives an alkene. What changes between the two?
quiz.answer: The hydroxide acts as a nucleophile in water and as a base in ethanol.
choices: The hydroxide acts as a nucleophile in water and as a base in ethanol.
The bromine departs as a radical in ethanol but as an ion in water.
The ethanol attacks the carbon itself, and the alkene follows from that product.
Water raises the temperature enough to force substitution instead.
quiz.explain: Solvent choice tips the competition between substitution and elimination: aqueous conditions favour attack at carbon, ethanolic conditions favour removal of a proton.

nodes.title: Inorganic Chemistry
nodes.goal: Coordination compounds and the elements in depth.
