quiz.prompt: In the coordination complex [Cu(NH3)4](2+), ammonia (NH3) acts as a monodentate ligand. What is the coordination number of the copper center?
quiz.explain: Four monodentate NH3 ligands each donate one lone pair, giving copper a coordination number of 4.

quiz.prompt: Many transition-metal coordination complexes are brightly colored. What is the usual origin of this color?
quiz.answer: Electrons absorbing light as they jump between split d-orbitals
quiz.explain: Ligand fields split the metal d-orbitals; d-d transitions absorb certain visible wavelengths, so the complex shows the complementary color, not the absorbed one.
choices: Electrons jumping between the metal's s and p orbitals, far apart in energy
The metal ion emitting light as its excited electrons fall back down again
The complex transmitting exactly the wavelengths that its d orbitals absorb
Electrons absorbing light as they jump between split d-orbitals

quiz.prompt: In the complex ion [Fe(CN)6](3-), each cyanide carries a -1 charge. What is the oxidation state of the iron?
quiz.explain: Six CN- contribute -6; for the overall -3 charge, iron must be +3 (since +3 - 6 = -3).

quiz.prompt: Ethylenediamine (en) binds a metal through both of its nitrogen atoms. State the coordination number of the cobalt in [Co(en)3](3+).
quiz.explain: Each bidentate en ligand donates two lone pairs, so three of them occupy 3 × 2 = 6 coordination sites.

quiz.prompt: [Ni(H2O)6](2+) is green; adding concentrated ammonia turns the solution blue-violet as [Ni(NH3)6](2+) forms. Explain the colour change in crystal-field terms.
quiz.answer: Ammonia splits the d orbitals further, so the complex absorbs shorter wavelengths
choices: Ammonia oxidises the nickel, changing how many d electrons are available to jump
Ammonia splits the d orbitals further, so the complex absorbs shorter wavelengths
Ammonia lowers the splitting, so the complex absorbs at longer wavelengths
The blue-violet is the colour absorbed, not the colour transmitted
quiz.explain: Ammonia sits above water in the spectrochemical series, so Δoct grows, the d-d absorption moves to shorter wavelength, and the transmitted colour shifts.

quiz.prompt: Group 2 sulfates grow less soluble down the group, while group 2 hydroxides grow more soluble. A student concludes that one of the two data sets must be a misprint. Diagnose the error in that reasoning.
quiz.answer: Lattice and hydration enthalpies fall at different rates down the group
choices: Both anions are the same size, so both trends must move the same way
Barium compounds weigh more, and heavier salts dissolve less readily
The hydroxide figures must be wrong, since one trend governs a whole group
Lattice and hydration enthalpies fall at different rates down the group
quiz.explain: With the large sulfate anion, hydration enthalpy falls faster than lattice enthalpy going down; with the small hydroxide anion the balance tips the other way.

quiz.prompt: A high-spin octahedral Fe3+ complex has a d5 configuration. How many unpaired d electrons does it carry?
quiz.explain: In the high-spin case each of the five d orbitals takes one electron, so all five are unpaired.

quiz.prompt: In the complex ion [PtCl4]2-, each chloride carries a charge of -1. What is the oxidation state of the platinum? Give it as a positive number.
quiz.explain: Four chlorides give -4; for an overall -2 the platinum must be +2.

quiz.prompt: Adding excess ammonia to copper(II) sulfate solution first gives a pale blue precipitate, which then dissolves to a deep blue solution. What has happened in the second step?
quiz.answer: Ligand exchange: ammonia has replaced water around the copper.
choices: Ligand exchange: ammonia has replaced water around the copper.
The copper has been reduced to copper(I) by the ammonia.
The hydroxide has redissolved in excess base, as an amphoteric one does.
Sulfate ions have entered the coordination sphere of the copper.
quiz.explain: Excess ammonia substitutes for water ligands to form the deep blue tetraamminediaquacopper(II) ion. Copper(II) hydroxide is not amphoteric, so excess base alone would not redissolve it.

quiz.prompt: Two compounds of formula [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] are isolated; one is a widely used anticancer drug and the other is inactive. What distinguishes them?
quiz.answer: They are cis and trans geometric isomers.
choices: They are cis and trans geometric isomers.
One holds platinum in a higher oxidation state.
They differ in how many chloride ligands are bound.
They are optical isomers, non-superimposable mirror images.
quiz.explain: Square-planar complexes with two pairs of ligands come in cis and trans forms; only the cis isomer binds DNA in the way that gives the drug its activity. A square-planar MA2B2 complex has a mirror plane, so it has no optical isomers.

nodes.title: Analytical Chemistry
nodes.goal: How chemists identify and measure substances.

quiz.prompt: Paper chromatography separates a mixture by how strongly each component is held by the stationary phase against how strongly it is carried by the mobile phase. A plant extract is run, and one pigment travels close to the solvent front while another barely leaves the baseline. What does that tell you about the two pigments?
quiz.answer: The fast one is held less by the paper and carried more by the solvent
quiz.explain: Rf is a ratio of affinities, not a mass or an amount. A pigment that partitions into the mobile phase spends more time moving and ends up near the front.
choices: The fast one is the lighter molecule, since mass alone sets how far a spot runs
The fast one is present in the larger amount, so its spot is pushed further along
The fast one is held less by the paper and carried more by the solvent
The fast one is the more soluble in water, whatever solvent is actually running

quiz.prompt: An infrared spectrum shows absorption where the light matches a vibrational energy gap of a bond, so each functional group has its own band. Two samples give infrared spectra that overlay exactly, yet they melt at different temperatures. What is the soundest reading of that?
quiz.answer: They carry the same functional groups, which infrared alone cannot separate
quiz.explain: Infrared reports which bonds are present, not how the whole molecule is put together. Isomers, or a pure sample against an impure one, can match in the infrared and still melt differently.
choices: One spectrum means one substance, so a spectrum must have been mislabelled
They carry the same functional groups, which infrared alone cannot separate
They are the same compound, and one of the melting points was measured badly
Melting point depends on structure, while infrared reports only the elements

quiz.prompt: In a titration, 25.0 mL of NaOH is exactly neutralized by 25.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl, reacting 1:1. What is the molar concentration of the NaOH solution, in mol/L?
quiz.explain: Equal volumes react 1:1, so moles of NaOH equal moles of HCl and the NaOH concentration is 0.100 M.

quiz.prompt: A coloured solution reads an absorbance of 0.60 in a 1.00 cm cell, and its molar absorptivity is 6000 L/(mol·cm). Using A = εcl, calculate the concentration in mol/L.
A mass spectrum shows a molecular ion at m/z 78 together with a peak at m/z 80 about one third as tall. What does that pair of peaks tell you?
quiz.answer: One chlorine, since chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 run about three to one
choices: One bromine, since bromine also produces a peak two mass units further up
Two compounds in the sample, one of them two mass units the heavier
One chlorine, since chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 run about three to one
A fragment that has picked up two extra hydrogen atoms somewhere along the way
quiz.explain: Bromine would give an M+2 peak of nearly equal height, because its two isotopes are about 1:1. The 3:1 ratio is the signature of a single chlorine.

quiz.prompt: Two analysts measure the same copper solution by colorimetry. One reads it off a calibration curve built from five standards; the other takes a single absorbance and assumes strict proportionality. Their answers differ by 15 percent. Judge whose method is sounder, and why.
quiz.answer: The curve, because it maps the instrument's real response
choices: The curve, because it maps the instrument's real response
The single reading, because fewer measurements leave fewer chances to slip
The single reading, because absorbance stays strictly proportional at any concentration
Either is fine, since the two must agree to within experimental error
quiz.explain: Beer's law is a limiting law: at higher concentrations the response bends away from a straight line. A curve built from standards captures that; an assumed constant does not.

quiz.prompt: A 20.0 mL sample of sulfuric acid needs 25.0 mL of 0.200 M sodium hydroxide to reach the end point, with 2 mol of base per mol of acid. What is the acid's concentration, in mol/L?
quiz.explain: Moles of base = 0.0250 x 0.200 = 0.00500; acid = half that = 0.00250 mol in 0.0200 L, giving 0.125 M.

quiz.prompt: Beer's law gives A = e c l. With e = 2500 L/(mol cm), l = 1.00 cm and c = 4.0e-4 mol/L, what is the absorbance?
A polar dye run on a TLC plate with a nonpolar solvent barely leaves the baseline. Which change raises its Rf value?
quiz.answer: Run the plate in a more polar mobile phase.
choices: Run the plate in a more polar mobile phase.
Run the plate for longer in the same solvent.
Use a thicker layer of the same stationary phase.
Develop the plate at a lower temperature.
quiz.explain: A polar solute clings to the polar stationary phase; a more polar eluent competes for it and carries it further up the plate.

quiz.prompt: A weak acid is titrated with a strong base, and the pH at half-neutralisation is read off the curve. What does that pH give directly?
quiz.answer: The pKa of the acid.
choices: The pKa of the acid.
The pH at the equivalence point.
The concentration of the acid.
The buffer capacity at the start of the titration.
quiz.explain: At half-neutralisation the acid and its conjugate base are equal in concentration, so the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives pH = pKa.

nodes.title: Quantum Chemistry
nodes.goal: Orbitals from the Schrödinger equation.

quiz.prompt: In quantum chemistry, what does the square of a wavefunction (|ψ|^2) at a point in space represent?
quiz.answer: The probability density for the electron at that point
quiz.explain: Born's interpretation says |ψ|^2 gives the probability density for locating the electron, not a definite orbit.
choices: The precise path that the electron follows in space
The exact speed of the electron at that point in space
The energy the electron has when it is found at that point
The probability density for the electron at that point

quiz.prompt: When two atomic orbitals combine in molecular orbital theory, they form two molecular orbitals. What are they?
quiz.answer: A lower-energy bonding and a higher-energy antibonding orbital
quiz.explain: Combining N atomic orbitals yields N molecular orbitals; two orbitals give a bonding (in-phase) and an antibonding (out-of-phase) pair.
choices: A bonding orbital and a non-bonding one left at the original energy
A lower-energy bonding and a higher-energy antibonding orbital
Two identical orbitals of exactly the same energy as before
Two antibonding orbitals, both above the original atomic energy

quiz.prompt: Molecular orbital theory defines bond order as (bonding electrons - antibonding electrons) / 2. For O2, there are 10 electrons in bonding orbitals and 6 in antibonding orbitals. What is the bond order?
quiz.explain: Bond order = (10 - 6) / 2 = 2, matching the double bond in O2.

quiz.prompt: The n = 3 shell holds 3s, 3p and 3d subshells. Counting all three, how many electrons can this shell hold in total?
quiz.explain: 2 in the s subshell, 6 in the p and 10 in the d gives 18, which matches the 2n² rule for n = 3.

quiz.prompt: Hund's rule says that electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before any one orbital takes a second electron. Apply it to a ground-state iron(II) ion, [Ar]3d6, in a weak ligand field: how many unpaired electrons does it carry?
quiz.answer: Four: one 3d orbital must take a pair, and four stay singly filled
choices: Six, since Hund's rule keeps all six of the d electrons unpaired
Four: one 3d orbital must take a pair, and four stay singly filled
Two, since the electrons pair off as soon as an orbital is available
Zero, since an even number of d electrons must all be paired up
quiz.explain: Six electrons into five orbitals: the first five go in singly and the sixth must double up somewhere, leaving 4 unpaired. That is why high-spin Fe(II) is strongly paramagnetic.

quiz.prompt: He2 would put two electrons in σ and two in σ*, while He2+ has two in σ and one in σ*. Predict which of the two can exist, and why.
quiz.answer: He2+, whose bond order of one half leaves net bonding
choices: Neither, since noble gases refuse to bond
He2+, whose bond order of one half leaves net bonding
He2, because filling the antibonding orbital adds extra stability
Both equally, since bond order counts only the electrons that bond
quiz.explain: He2 has bond order (2−2)/2 = 0 and falls apart; He2+ has (2−1)/2 = 0.5 and is observed in discharges. Antibonding electrons subtract, they do not stabilise.

quiz.prompt: Using molecular orbital theory, what is the bond order of the N2 molecule?
quiz.explain: N2 has eight bonding and two antibonding valence electrons, giving (8 - 2)/2 = 3.

quiz.prompt: The n = 4 shell contains 4s, 4p, 4d and 4f subshells. How many orbitals is that in total?
quiz.explain: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 orbitals, which is n squared.

quiz.prompt: Nitrogen has a far higher bond dissociation energy than oxygen, and oxygen is drawn to a magnet while nitrogen is not. Which model accounts for both facts at once?
quiz.answer: Molecular orbital theory, with two unpaired electrons in oxygen's π* orbitals.
choices: Lewis structures, which give oxygen a double bond with all electrons paired.
Molecular orbital theory, with two unpaired electrons in oxygen's π* orbitals.
Resonance between two Lewis structures, one of them with unpaired electrons.
Valence bond theory using sp hybrid orbitals on both atoms.
quiz.explain: Only the MO picture predicts oxygen's two unpaired pi-star electrons, explaining both its paramagnetism and its lower bond order.

quiz.prompt: A student fills the 4s orbital before the 3d in a neutral scandium atom, then removes 4s electrons first when forming Sc3+. Assess the reasoning.
quiz.answer: Both steps are right as written.
choices: Both steps are right as written.
The filling order is right, but 3d electrons should leave first.
The filling order is wrong: 3d fills before 4s in every atom.
Neither: scandium's 4s orbital is empty in the neutral atom.
quiz.explain: 4s fills before 3d in the neutral atom, and once the d orbitals are occupied the 4s electrons become the higher in energy and are lost first.

nodes.title: Electrochemistry
nodes.goal: Batteries, corrosion and electrolysis.

quiz.prompt: In any electrochemical cell, which process always occurs at the cathode?
quiz.answer: Reduction, the gain of electrons
quiz.explain: By definition, reduction takes place at the cathode in both galvanic and electrolytic cells. Which electrode is the negative one does change between the two, but the definition does not.
choices: Reduction in a galvanic cell, but oxidation in an electrolytic one
Reduction, the gain of electrons
Oxidation, the loss of electrons
Whatever happens at the negative electrode, in either kind of cell

quiz.prompt: A galvanic (voltaic) cell produces electricity spontaneously. What does this imply about its overall cell potential and Gibbs energy?
quiz.answer: The cell potential is positive and ΔG is negative
quiz.explain: A spontaneous cell has E_cell > 0, and since ΔG = -nFE, ΔG is negative.
choices: The cell potential is positive but ΔG is also positive
The cell potential is positive and ΔG is negative
The cell potential is negative and ΔG is positive
Both the cell potential and ΔG are zero

quiz.prompt: Iron rusts faster when in contact with a less reactive metal like copper, but is protected when connected to a more reactive metal like zinc. Why does the zinc protect the iron?
quiz.answer: Zinc oxidizes more readily and corrodes first, sparing the iron
quiz.explain: Being more reactive, zinc gives up electrons preferentially and is consumed, protecting the iron by cathodic (sacrificial) protection.
choices: Zinc oxidizes more readily and corrodes first, sparing the iron
Zinc coats the iron in a layer of its own oxide that seals the surface
Zinc makes the surrounding iron more easily oxidized than usual
Zinc conducts the electrons away from the iron so that none are lost

quiz.prompt: Standard electrode potentials are Cu2+/Cu = +0.34 V and Zn2+/Zn = −0.76 V. Calculate the standard cell potential, in volts, of a zinc-copper galvanic cell.
quiz.explain: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V, and the positive sign confirms the cell runs on its own.

quiz.prompt: Molten aluminium oxide is electrolysed, and Al(3+) ions are discharged at the cathode. How many moles of electrons must pass to deposit one mole of aluminium?
quiz.explain: Al³⁺ + 3 e⁻ → Al, so three moles of electrons deposit one mole of aluminium. That charge cost is why aluminium smelting is so power-hungry.

quiz.prompt: Electrolysing concentrated brine gives chlorine at the anode, even though the potentials say oxygen should be discharged first. Choose the best explanation.
quiz.answer: Chloride is concentrated, and oxygen has a large overpotential on the anode
choices: Chloride ions carry their charge to the anode faster than water molecules can
Sodium ions crowd the anode and keep water away from the surface
Chloride is oxidised more easily than water, as the standard potentials show
Chloride is concentrated, and oxygen has a large overpotential on the anode
quiz.explain: Thermodynamics ranks the half-reactions and puts water first; kinetics decides the outcome, because oxygen evolution is slow on most anodes and concentrated chloride tips the balance further.

quiz.prompt: How many coulombs of charge pass when a current of 2.00 A flows for 300 s?
Using the Faraday constant 96500 C/mol, how many moles of electrons does 193000 C correspond to?
quiz.explain: 193000 / 96500 = 2 mol of electrons.

quiz.prompt: A steel ship's hull carries bolted-on blocks of magnesium below the waterline. What are they for?
quiz.answer: To corrode in place of the steel.
choices: To corrode in place of the steel.
To carry the current that keeps the hull negatively charged.
To insulate the steel hull.
To react with the seawater and use up its dissolved oxygen.
quiz.explain: Sacrificial protection: magnesium is more readily oxidised, so it supplies the electrons and corrodes while the iron is spared. No external current is involved, which is what separates it from impressed-current protection.

quiz.prompt: Electrolysing dilute sulfuric acid with inert electrodes gives hydrogen and oxygen in a volume ratio of two to one. What accounts for the ratio?
quiz.answer: Each mole of oxygen needs four electrons while each mole of hydrogen needs two.
choices: Each mole of oxygen needs four electrons while each mole of hydrogen needs two.
Hydrogen molecules are lighter, so they take up twice the volume.
The acid supplies twice as much hydrogen as the water does.
Oxygen dissolves in the solution, halving the amount collected.
quiz.explain: The same charge passes at both electrodes, and the half-equations require twice as many electrons per mole of oxygen as per mole of hydrogen.

nodes.title: Advanced Biochemistry
nodes.goal: The chemistry of life's macromolecules.

quiz.prompt: A protein of a single polypeptide chain is heated until its helices and sheets unravel completely, then cooled slowly, whereupon it recovers full activity. Its peptide bonds were never broken. What does that recovery establish?
quiz.answer: The amino-acid sequence alone holds enough information to specify the fold
quiz.explain: Primary structure is the sequence; unfolding and refolding without touching that sequence shows the fold is written into it. The stem rules out peptide-bond breakage, and one chain cannot have quaternary structure.
choices: Secondary structure survived the heating, and only the tertiary fold was lost
The amino-acid sequence alone holds enough information to specify the fold
The protein has quaternary structure, and its separate chains reassembled
Heating broke the peptide bonds, which then reformed in the same order

quiz.prompt: In Michaelis-Menten kinetics Vmax is the rate approached once substrate saturates every active site. A chemist raises the substrate concentration from 10 times Km to 20 times Km and finds the rate barely moves. Why not?
quiz.answer: At 10 Km the enzyme is already near saturation, so extra substrate finds no free site
quiz.explain: v = Vmax[S]/(Km+[S]) gives 0.909 Vmax at 10 Km and 0.952 Vmax at 20 Km, a rise of under 5 percent. The hyperbola has flattened; nearly every active site is already occupied.
choices: The extra substrate has started to inhibit the enzyme at that concentration
Once substrate is in excess the rate is fixed by Km rather than by Vmax
At 10 Km the enzyme is already near saturation, so extra substrate finds no free site
Doubling the substrate always doubles the rate, so the measurement must be wrong

quiz.prompt: A competitive inhibitor binds the active site of an enzyme. Compared with the uninhibited enzyme, how do the apparent Km and Vmax change?
quiz.answer: Apparent Km increases while Vmax stays the same
quiz.explain: A competitive inhibitor can be outcompeted by excess substrate, so Vmax is unchanged but more substrate is needed, raising apparent Km.
choices: Vmax decreases while Km stays the same
Both Km and Vmax decrease
Apparent Km increases while Vmax stays the same
Apparent Km decreases while Vmax stays the same

quiz.prompt: An enzyme obeying Michaelis-Menten kinetics has Km = 2.0 mM and Vmax = 100 µmol/min. Calculate the initial rate, in µmol/min, at a substrate concentration of 2.0 mM.
quiz.explain: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) = 100 × 2.0 / (2.0 + 2.0) = 50 µmol/min. At [S] = Km the enzyme runs at exactly half its maximum rate.

quiz.prompt: Two Lineweaver-Burk plots for one enzyme, with and without an inhibitor, cross exactly on the x-axis but differ in slope and in y-intercept. Identify the inhibition and its effect.
quiz.answer: Noncompetitive: Vmax falls, Km unchanged
choices: Noncompetitive: Vmax falls, Km unchanged
Competitive: apparent Km rises while Vmax holds steady
Uncompetitive: Km and Vmax both fall by the same factor
Substrate inhibition at high concentration, dragging both parameters down
quiz.explain: The x-intercept is −1/Km, so a shared x-intercept means Km is untouched; the raised y-intercept (1/Vmax) says Vmax has dropped. That is the classic noncompetitive signature.

quiz.prompt: The hydrophobic effect drives nonpolar side chains out of water and into a protein's core. A folded globular protein is transferred from water into a nonpolar solvent that does not break covalent bonds. Predict what happens to the fold.
quiz.answer: It turns itself inside out, burying the polar residues that had faced the water
choices: It holds the same fold, since the covalent backbone fixes the shape
It unravels into a random coil, the driving force having vanished
It packs tighter still, since a nonpolar solvent squeezes the core harder
It turns itself inside out, burying the polar residues that had faced the water
quiz.explain: The same rule applies with the phases swapped: whatever the solvent dislikes goes inside. Nonpolar side chains now face out and the polar ones are buried, so the structure inverts rather than unfolding.

quiz.prompt: An enzyme with Km = 5.0 mM and Vmax = 200 micromol/min is run at a substrate concentration of 15 mM. Give the initial rate, in micromol/min.
quiz.explain: v = Vmax [S]/(Km + [S]) = 200 x 15/20 = 150 micromol/min.

quiz.prompt: A polypeptide is 120 amino acids long. How many peptide bonds does the chain contain?
quiz.explain: Each bond joins two residues, so a chain of 120 residues has 119 bonds.

quiz.prompt: A protein from a hot-spring organism keeps its fold at 90 degrees Celsius, while its close relative from a temperate organism unfolds at 50. Which difference most plausibly accounts for that?
quiz.answer: More salt bridges and a tighter hydrophobic core.
choices: More salt bridges and a tighter hydrophobic core.
A longer chain, since extra length always stabilises a fold.
More glycine residues, which let the chain flex rather than break.
Fewer disulfide bonds, leaving the chain usefully looser.
quiz.explain: Thermostability comes from accumulated small stabilisations: ion pairs, tighter packing and better-shielded hydrophobic cores. Extra glycine does the opposite, buying flexibility at the cost of rigidity.

quiz.prompt: An inhibitor is found to lower both the apparent Vmax and the apparent Km of an enzyme by the same factor. Which mode of inhibition fits?
quiz.answer: Uncompetitive inhibition.
choices: Uncompetitive inhibition.
Competitive inhibition.
Noncompetitive inhibition, which leaves Km alone.
Irreversible covalent modification of the active site.
quiz.explain: An uncompetitive inhibitor binds only the enzyme-substrate complex, pulling both Vmax and Km down by the same factor and leaving Vmax/Km unchanged.

nodes.title: Materials Chemistry
nodes.goal: Polymers, nanomaterials and semiconductors.

quiz.prompt: Polymerisation joins many small monomer units into long chains. A chemist heats ethene (C2H4, molar mass 28 g/mol) under pressure with an initiator and isolates a waxy solid of average molar mass 30,000 g/mol. Which observation would best confirm the solid really is a polymer?
quiz.answer: It softens across a range of temperatures rather than melting at one sharp point
quiz.explain: A polymer sample is a spread of chain lengths, so it softens over a range instead of melting sharply. The average mass need not be an exact multiple of 28 precisely because it is an average.
choices: It burns in air, since only long-chain molecules will burn at all
It softens across a range of temperatures rather than melting at one sharp point
It is insoluble in water, which no small molecule ever is
Its molar mass is not a whole-number multiple of the monomer's 28 g/mol

quiz.prompt: Silicon is a semiconductor. Doping pure silicon with a small amount of phosphorus (which has one more valence electron) produces which type of material?
quiz.answer: An n-type semiconductor carrying extra mobile electrons
quiz.explain: Phosphorus donates an extra electron per atom, adding negative charge carriers to make n-type silicon. The crystal as a whole stays neutral: each donated electron leaves a fixed positive phosphorus ion behind.
choices: An n-type semiconductor carrying extra mobile electrons
A p-type semiconductor carrying extra positive holes
An n-type semiconductor that now carries a net negative charge
An insulator, since the impurity atoms disrupt the silicon lattice

quiz.prompt: Catalysis happens on the atoms at a nanoparticle's surface. A maker halves the diameter of its spherical gold nanoparticles while keeping the total mass of gold the same. Roughly what happens to the surface area available per gram?
quiz.answer: It doubles, since surface area per gram goes as one over the radius
quiz.explain: For a sphere, area/mass = 4πr² / (ρ·4/3πr³) = 3/(ρr). Halving r doubles the specific surface area, which is why a nanoscale catalyst offers so much more working surface per gram.
choices: It quadruples, since the surface area of a sphere goes as the radius squared
It doubles, since surface area per gram goes as one over the radius
It stays the same, since the total mass of gold has not changed
It halves, since each particle now carries less surface than before

quiz.prompt: A polyethylene sample has chains of average molar mass 28,000 g/mol, built from C2H4 repeat units of molar mass 28 g/mol. Calculate the average number of repeat units per chain.
quiz.explain: 28,000 ÷ 28 = 1000 repeat units, which is the average degree of polymerisation.

quiz.prompt: A cracked part moulded from a thermosetting resin reaches the workshop. An engineer proposes melting the pieces down and re-moulding them, as would work for a thermoplastic. Predict the outcome and give the reason.
quiz.answer: It fails: cross-links hold the chains, so the resin chars rather than flows
choices: It works, since heating any polymer above its softening point restores flow
It fails: cross-links hold the chains, so the resin chars rather than flows
It works, but only once fresh monomer is stirred into the melt
It fails: the resin has crystallised, and a crystal will not soften again
quiz.explain: A thermoset is one giant cross-linked network, so there are no separate chains to slide. Heat it enough and the covalent bonds decompose instead of melting.

quiz.prompt: Silicon has a band gap of 1.1 eV. Doping it with boron, which brings three valence electrons, raises its conductivity sharply at room temperature. Explain what boron adds to the band structure.
quiz.answer: Empty acceptor levels just above the valence band, giving mobile holes
choices: Empty acceptor levels just above the valence band, giving mobile holes
A narrower band gap, so that ordinary thermal energy carries electrons across
Spare electrons donated straight into the conduction band, as phosphorus does
A greater number of silicon atoms taking part in conduction than before
quiz.explain: Boron has one valence electron too few, so it accepts an electron from the valence band and leaves a hole behind. The gap itself is barely changed.

quiz.prompt: A polymer has a number-average molar mass of 45000 g/mol and is built from repeat units of 90 g/mol. What is the degree of polymerisation?
quiz.explain: 45000 / 90 = 500 repeat units per chain on average.

quiz.prompt: A cube of edge 10 nm is cut into cubes of edge 1 nm. By what factor does the total surface area increase?
quiz.explain: Cutting to one tenth of the edge length multiplies the total surface area by ten.

quiz.prompt: A stretched rubber band under a fixed load pulls shorter when it is warmed, while a metal wire under load lengthens. Which explanation fits the rubber?
quiz.answer: Coiling back regains entropy, and that pull grows with temperature.
choices: Coiling back regains entropy, and that pull grows with temperature.
The rubber's covalent bonds contract as the temperature rises.
Heating drives out absorbed water and shrinks the band.
The cross-links melt and let the chains slide back together.
quiz.explain: Rubber elasticity is entropic: the restoring force is proportional to temperature, so a hotter band pulls harder and contracts.

quiz.prompt: One batch of CdSe quantum dots emits green light and a batch of larger dots of the same material emits red. Explain the shift.
quiz.answer: Larger dots confine the carriers less, so the gap is smaller.
choices: Larger dots confine the carriers less, so the gap is smaller.
Larger dots hold more impurity atoms, and those glow red.
Larger dots scatter the shorter blue wavelengths away, leaving red.
The larger batch was simply grown at a higher temperature.
quiz.explain: Quantum confinement raises the effective band gap as the particle shrinks, so smaller dots emit at shorter wavelengths.

nodes.title: Computational Chemistry
nodes.goal: Simulating molecules on computers.

quiz.prompt: Molecular dynamics integrates Newton's equations for every atom, and the time step has to be short enough to resolve the fastest vibration in the system, which is about a femtosecond. A group wants to watch one millisecond of protein folding. Why is that so hard?
quiz.answer: A femtosecond step means about 10^12 steps, each recomputing every force
quiz.explain: 1 ms ÷ 1 fs = 10^12 steps. The step is set by bond vibrations, not by the process of interest, and that mismatch of twelve orders of magnitude is the central cost problem in the field.
choices: Newton's equations cannot be integrated beyond a few thousand steps
A femtosecond step means about 10^12 steps, each recomputing every force
Proteins fold too slowly for any classical force field to describe them
The Schrödinger equation has to be solved afresh at every one of the steps

quiz.prompt: Ab initio quantum chemistry methods and classical molecular dynamics differ in a key trade-off. What is it?
quiz.answer: Quantum methods are more accurate but costlier, limiting system size
quiz.explain: Quantum approaches capture electrons explicitly at high cost, while classical force fields trade electronic detail for the speed to handle large systems.
choices: Force fields treat electrons explicitly, while quantum methods average over them
Quantum methods are cheaper and handle larger systems than force fields
Quantum methods are more accurate but costlier, limiting system size
Classical dynamics reproduces bond breaking, which quantum methods cannot

quiz.prompt: A virtual screen docks a library of a million compounds into a target, ranks them, and chemists then make the top few hundred. Most of those turn out inactive. What makes the exercise worth running anyway?
quiz.answer: Even a few-fold enrichment over random picking saves years of synthesis
quiz.explain: Screening is a filter, not an oracle. Lifting the hit rate from one in ten thousand to one in a hundred is an enormous saving even though most ranked compounds still fail.
choices: The ranking is accurate enough that the true best binder is always near the top
Even a few-fold enrichment over random picking saves years of synthesis
Docking scores are true free energies, so the top of the list needs no testing
Synthesis is cheap next to computing time, so the order hardly matters

quiz.prompt: A molecular dynamics run advances in 2 femtosecond steps. How many steps does 1 nanosecond of simulated motion take?
quiz.explain: 1 ns = 10⁶ fs, and 10⁶ ÷ 2 = 500,000 steps. The tiny step is set by the fastest vibrations, which is why long simulations are so costly.

quiz.prompt: Two groups compute the same reaction barrier. One uses DFT with a small basis set and reports 60 kJ/mol; the other uses coupled cluster with a large basis set and reports 85 kJ/mol, matching experiment. Choose the best account of the gap.
quiz.answer: The DFT number carries error from both the functional and the small basis set
choices: Barrier heights depend on which software package was used to run them
The DFT number carries error from both the functional and the small basis set
The experiment must be at fault, since DFT solves the electronic problem exactly
Coupled cluster overshoots barriers, so the true value sits below 60 kJ/mol
quiz.explain: DFT is exact in principle but approximate in practice, because the exchange-correlation functional is approximate; a small basis set adds a second error on top.

quiz.prompt: A docking program ranks one molecule as the strongest binder in a library, but the assay shows no measurable affinity. Which limitation most likely explains the miss?
quiz.answer: Scoring functions treat solvation and entropy far too crudely
choices: Docking returns a real binding constant, so the assay must be at fault
The rank is only wrong if the pose is wrong, and poses are usually right
The compound is probably insoluble, which docking is designed to detect
Scoring functions treat solvation and entropy far too crudely
quiz.explain: Docking scores are fast empirical approximations, not free energies. Desolvation and conformational entropy are exactly where they are weakest, so a correct pose can still carry a badly wrong score.

quiz.prompt: A molecular dynamics run advances in steps of 1 femtosecond. How many steps are needed to simulate 5 picoseconds?
quiz.explain: 1 ps is 1000 fs, so 5 ps is 5000 steps.

quiz.prompt: A quantum chemistry method scales as the cube of the number of basis functions. By what factor does the cost rise when the basis set is doubled?
quiz.explain: 2 cubed = 8 times the cost.

quiz.prompt: A coarse-grained simulation of a lipid bilayer reproduces the membrane thickness well but not the hydrogen-bond network at the surface. What does that show?
quiz.answer: Coarse graining trades chemical detail for reach in size and time.
choices: Coarse graining trades chemical detail for reach in size and time.
The force field must contain an arithmetic mistake.
The simulation was simply run for too short a time.
Hydrogen bonding cannot be captured by classical force fields of any kind.
quiz.explain: Grouping atoms into beads deliberately discards the detail that hydrogen bonding depends on, in exchange for far larger and longer simulations.

quiz.prompt: Two conformers computed in the gas phase differ by 15 kJ/mol, yet experiments in water find them almost equally populated. What has most likely been left out?
quiz.answer: Solvation was not modelled.
choices: Solvation was not modelled.
The basis set lacked polarisation functions.
Zero-point vibrational energy was omitted.
The SCF never converged.
quiz.explain: A polar solvent can stabilise one conformer far more than the other, so gas-phase energies can be badly misleading for solution behaviour.

nodes.title: Frontiers of Chemistry
nodes.goal: Catalysis, green chemistry and molecular machines.

quiz.prompt: A catalyst opens a route of lower activation energy and is regenerated at the end of each cycle. A student proposes using one to drive a reaction with ΔG > 0 through to completion. What is wrong with the plan?
quiz.answer: A catalyst changes the rate, not the position: an uphill reaction stays uphill
quiz.explain: Lowering the barrier speeds both directions equally, so the equilibrium position is untouched. Getting an uphill reaction to run needs coupling to something downhill, not a catalyst.
choices: A catalyst changes the rate, not the position: an uphill reaction stays uphill
It would work, but only if enough catalyst is added to match the reactant
Catalysts speed only reactions that are already fast, and this one is not
The catalyst would be used up, since driving an uphill reaction consumes it

quiz.prompt: Green chemistry ranks preventing waste and hazard above cleaning them up afterwards. A plant swaps a route running in dichloromethane at reflux (atom economy 40 percent, 3 steps) for one running in water at 40 degrees Celsius (atom economy 35 percent, 4 steps) at the same yield. Which reading is fairest?
quiz.answer: A real gain in solvent hazard and energy, paid for in atom economy and steps
quiz.explain: The twelve principles pull against each other and have to be traded off. Dropping a chlorinated solvent and reflux heating is a genuine gain; losing five points of atom economy and adding a step is a genuine cost.
choices: A clear loss, since atom economy is the measure green chemistry actually uses
A real gain in solvent hazard and energy, paid for in atom economy and steps
A clear gain, since a route that runs in water is green whatever else it does
No change either way, because the yield is what matters and it is unchanged

quiz.prompt: A rotaxane motor's ring is driven around its axle by pulses of chemical fuel. Between pulses, thermal motion on its own would let the ring drift either way round. What must the fuel pulses supply for net one-way circulation?
quiz.answer: Energy that makes the reverse step over one barrier far slower than the forward step
quiz.explain: Thermal motion alone cannot produce net directed work, or the second law would fall. Directionality comes from spending energy to make one crossing kinetically much cheaper than its reverse.
choices: A steady push in one direction, in the way a current flows through a wire
Enough heat to lift the ring over every barrier on the axle at once
Energy that makes the reverse step over one barrier far slower than the forward step
A magnetic alignment that fixes which end of the axle counts as the front

quiz.prompt: Ethanol can be made by fermenting glucose: C6H12O6 -> 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2. With molar masses C6H12O6 = 180, C2H5OH = 46 and CO2 = 44, calculate the percentage atom economy for ethanol, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Atom economy = mass of wanted product ÷ total mass of reactants × 100 = (2 × 46)/180 × 100 = 51.1 percent. Nearly half the mass of the sugar leaves as carbon dioxide rather than ending up in the ethanol.

quiz.prompt: A heterogeneous catalyst for ammonia synthesis loses most of its activity after traces of sulfur compounds enter the feed gas. Choose the best account of the poisoning.
quiz.answer: Sulfur adsorbs strongly on the active sites and blocks them
choices: Sulfur adsorbs strongly on the active sites and blocks them
Sulfur reacts with the ammonia and destroys the product as it forms
Sulfur raises the activation energy of the gas-phase reaction itself
Sulfur shifts the equilibrium constant so that less ammonia can form
quiz.explain: Heterogeneous catalysis happens on a small number of surface sites. Sulfur binds them tightly, so reactant molecules have nowhere to adsorb.

quiz.prompt: A light-driven molecular motor has to turn in one direction rather than jiggle back and forth at random. What feature makes directional rotation possible?
quiz.answer: A ratchet of energy-driven steps that blocks off the reverse path
choices: Its large mass, which stops thermal motion from reversing the turn
A chiral centre, which by itself fixes which way the molecule turns
A ratchet of energy-driven steps that blocks off the reverse path
Brownian motion by itself, which happens to favour one direction
quiz.explain: Thermal motion alone cannot produce net directed work, or the second law would fall. Chirality biases the shape of the barriers but cannot by itself drive rotation; directionality needs energy input plus irreversible steps.

quiz.prompt: A catalyst lowers a barrier from 100 to 75 kJ/mol. Using k proportional to exp(-Ea/RT) with R = 8.314 J/(mol K) and T = 300 K, what is the rate enhancement factor, to the nearest thousand?
quiz.explain: exp(25000/(8.314 x 300)) = exp(10.02) = 2.25e4, which is 23000 to the nearest thousand.

quiz.prompt: Atom economy is the mass of the desired product divided by the total mass of the reactants, as a percentage. A reaction uses 40 g and 60 g of two reactants and yields 72 g of the desired product. What is the atom economy, as a percentage?
A pharmaceutical route is redesigned to run in water at 40 degrees Celsius instead of in dichloromethane at reflux, at the same yield. Which green-chemistry gain is the most direct?
quiz.answer: A safer solvent and less energy used.
choices: A safer solvent and less energy used.
A higher atom economy for that step.
